#10291. How to Migrate an Elementor Site to the WordPress Block Editor

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Elementor made your site easy to build. It may also be making it slow. Here's how to move a site onto the Block Editor without breaking URLs, losing content or dropping out of Google.

Page builders solved a real problem. Before the Block Editor matured, they were the easiest way to give clients drag-and-drop layouts. Many of those sites are still running today, and a lot of them are slow on phones.

The data backs that up. According to the HTTP Archive Core Web Vitals Technology Report for June 2026, 36.8% of Elementor sites pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Sites built with the Block Editor pass 53.0% of the time. That's correlation, not proof, since hosting and setup matter too. But in my experience, it matches what happens when you remove the builder from a slow site.

My reason for migrating sites off Elementor is simple: **page builders make websites heavy. **Having said that, Elementor has improved a lot. Its performance settings, Flexbox Containers, and asset-loading options cut much of the bloat, and a carefully tuned Elementor site can pass Core Web Vitals. But tuning only goes so far. You’re still shipping the builder’s framework, wrapper markup and scripts, and every plugin or Elementor update is a chance for the speed to slip again.

For small business sites that don’t need drag-and-drop editing, rebuilding the same design on the WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg) removes that weight at the source, without changing what the client sees.

This guide follows the order I use. It assumes you're comfortable with WordPress admin, WP-CLI and a staging site. If you need to set those up first, SitePoint's guide to the ultimate WordPress development environment covers the tooling.

Not every Elementor site needs to move. Migration makes sense when:

It's harder to justify when the site leans on Elementor Pro features you'd need to replace, such as complex popups, dynamic loops or WooCommerce templates. Those can all be rebuilt, but the job gets bigger fast.

You can't prove a migration worked without "before" numbers. Capture these on the live site first.

Crawl the site with a tool such as Screaming Frog, and export every indexable URL with its title, meta description, H1 and canonical tag. You can also pull published pages and posts with WP-CLI:

Run Google PageSpeed Insights, which uses Lighthouse for its lab scores, on the homepage and two or three key templates. Save the mobile lab scores and, if the site has enough traffic, the field data from real users.

Export the last three months of pages and queries from Google Search Console. That's what you'll compare against after launch.

Elementor stores each page's layout as JSON in the elementordata post meta field, and marks builder pages with elementoredit_mode. This command lists every page that uses the builder:

Then list everything else Elementor controls, which is easy to miss:

On the small business sites I've migrated, the inventory usually turns up more than the owner expects. The pages are the easy part. The surprises are saved templates nobody remembers creating, a popup still running on every page, add-on widgets from plugins that were installed once and forgotten, and contact forms that live inside Elementor Pro rather than a form plugin. Finding those before the rebuild saves a broken launch.

Work on a staging copy. Install a block theme, such as Twenty Twenty-Five or a lightweight starter theme, and move the Elementor global styles into theme.json. That way colors, fonts and spacing are defined once, instead of in every widget.

Copy the hex values and font names from Elementor's Site Settings so the new site matches the old one. Rebuild the header and footer as template parts in the Site Editor. If you'd rather write a theme yourself, SitePoint's series on building a WordPress theme from scratch covers the basics.

Most Elementor sites repeat the same few sections: a hero, a services grid, testimonials and a call to action. Build each one once as a block pattern, then reuse it on every page. Patterns are plain block markup, so you don't need React to write them, whatever you may have heard about React and WordPress development.

In a block theme, any PHP file in the /patterns folder with a header comment is registered automatically:

For page content, there's a useful shortcut. Elementor saves a plain HTML copy of each page into post_content. Open a page in the Block Editor, and the old content usually appears in a Classic block. Choose Convert to blocks, then delete the leftovers and rebuild the layout with your patterns. It keeps the copy and images, so you only redo the design.

The difference shows up in the page source. Here's typical front-end markup for a single heading on an Elementor page, using the older section and column layout:

Newer Elementor versions with Flexbox containers and the optimized markup settings trim some of those wrappers, but most older sites still carry all of them. Multiply that by every element on every page, and the weight adds up.

To speed up this step, I built a free Elementor to Gutenberg converter. Paste in a page's elementordata JSON from Step 2, and it returns block markup you can paste into the Block Editor's code editor. It handles headings, text, images, buttons, spacers, dividers and column layouts, and lists anything it can't convert, such as forms and popups, for you to rebuild by hand. It runs entirely in your browser, so the page data never leaves your computer.

The code is rarely what holds a migration up. Content is. Once clients see their site being rebuilt, many decide it's time to rewrite their pages too, and the project ends up waiting on copywriters and approvals. My fix is to separate the two: migrate the existing content as it is, launch, then update the copy afterwards. That keeps the speed and SEO gains on schedule, and it means any ranking change can be traced to either the migration or the new copy, not both at once.

This is the step that decides whether rankings hold.

To spot-check a redirect or a status code from the command line:

When staging matches the live site, deploy it. Then:

Leave the old elementordata meta in place for a few weeks, in case you need to roll back. Once you're confident, take a backup and remove it to shrink the database.

Run PageSpeed Insights again straight away for lab scores. Field data takes longer: the Chrome UX Report uses a rolling 28-day window, so give it a month before judging real-user results. Compare Search Console clicks for the same period before and after launch.

In my migrations, the biggest change is usually page weight and loading time, because the builder's CSS, JavaScript and wrapper markup are gone. What doesn't always improve is server response time. If the site is on slow shared hosting, the first byte still arrives late, and that needs a hosting fix, not a rebuild. Search traffic should hold steady if the URLs and metadata were protected. If it drops, the Step 5 crawl comparison is the first place to look.

Moving off Elementor isn't a one-click job, but it isn't a full redesign either. Record a baseline, inventory what the builder controls, rebuild with patterns, and protect every URL. Most of the speed gain comes from removing code the site never needed. For what to tackle after that, see these practical web performance techniques. Most of the risk comes from rushing the SEO checks. Done carefully, the client gets the same site, a faster one, and an editor that comes with WordPress itself.

***Author Bio: ***Fahad Raza is a WordPress developer and SEO consultant based in Sydney. He has built websites since 2005, worked in SEO for more than 18 years, and spent eight and a half years on the IKEA Australia and New Zealand website.

Air travelers in the U.S. were in for a nasty surprise last Friday night after the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) called for a nationwide ground stop. According to the Wall Street Journal, the issue started after a newly installed Juniper router, built by HP Enterprise, started broadcasting to a wide part of the network. This, in turn, overloaded the established and antiquated system, resulting in communications glitches and interruptions between air traffic control and pilots.

Thankfully, this did not affect other safety services, like Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS), which primarily relied on hardware in aircraft that communicated with other transponders to help prevent accidents. Still, air traffic’s inability to communicate with high-flying aircraft made it impossible to coordinate the thousands of airborne aircraft at any given time, forcing the agency to call for an emergency ground stop. A nationwide ground stop order is quite a drastic move, and it has only been invoked twice before. The first such event was on September 11, 2001, when terrorists infamously used hijacked airliners as weapons. The second was on January 11, 2023, when the agency’s Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system, which sends warnings to pilots and air crews of important information crucial to flight safety, suffered from an outage for about a couple of hours.

The problem first became apparent at Indianapolis Center, which monitors the airspace in northern Kentucky, southern Indiana, southern Ohio, and parts of West Virginia, when the personnel working at the site had trouble communicating with flight crews. The agency then went on a nationwide hunt for the glitch, and it soon found two possible sources — an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Upon deeper inspection, the agency discovered that new routers recently installed in both places have begun sending out a high volume of data across the entire FAA communications network.

“We saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate, a thousand connections over every four to five seconds,” FAA technology chief Rebecca Guy said in a press conference. This might seem like a minor hiccup for any modern network, which could typically handle connections in the hundreds of thousands, or even millions, per second. For example, one of the largest recorded DDoS attacks for 2026 saw traffic spike to 31.4 TB/s, which is enough to takedown an entire country’s web infrastructure.

However, the FAA still uses an antiquated copper network, which was easily overwhelmed by the amount of data that the routers sent. This network is already several decades old, so the agency is currently in the process of upgrading everything to fiber, which is costing taxpayers billions of dollars. Even as the agency is in this period of transition, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has raised several questions. “Was it a faulty installation? Was it a faulty configuration? Or was it just a bad piece of router technology that we put into this system that propagated these errors?” Bedford said in statement on Saturday. He also added that the agency is investigating the incident. As for the Juniper router, an HPE spokesperson said that they appear to be working as intended and that “They did not fail.” It was eventually discovered that a specific feature on the router caused the system overload, with FAA employees turning it off across the entire network on all Juniper routers.

It took about four hours for the FAA to return its communications network to normal, but repercussions go way beyond that. Passengers aboard all those canceled and diverted flights needed to be served, even as new passengers kept on arriving for their scheduled flights. It’s been estimated that airlines needed a few days to recover after the CrowdStrike crash of 2024 forced United, Delta, and American Airlines to cancel flights (except for Southwest, which avoided the chaos because it used an antiquated OS from the 1990s), so we expect passengers unlucky enough to be in transit during this incident to suffer waits between a few hours to a day or two before their journeys could continue.

#10288. Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v5.4 update, you can now encode and compare texts, images, audio, and videos using the same familiar API. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use these new multimodal capabilities for both embedding and reranking.

Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs. This opens up use cases like visual document retrieval, cross-modal search, and multimodal RAG pipelines.

If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

Traditional embedding models convert text into fixed-size vectors. Multimodal embedding models extend this by mapping inputs from different modalities (text, images, audio, or video) into a shared embedding space. This means you can compare a text query against image documents (or vice versa) using the same similarity functions you're already familiar with.

Similarly, traditional reranker (Cross Encoder) models compute relevance scores between pairs of texts. Multimodal rerankers can score pairs where one or both elements are images, combined text-image documents, or other modalities.

For example, you can compare a text query against image documents, find video clips matching a description, or build RAG pipelines that work across modalities.

Multimodal models require some extra dependencies. Install the extras for the modalities you need (see Installation for more details):

VLM-based models like Qwen3-VL-2B require a GPU with at least ~8 GB of VRAM. For the 8B variants, expect ~20 GB. If you don't have a local GPU, consider using a cloud GPU service or Google Colab. On CPU, these models will be extremely slow; text-only or CLIP models are better suited for CPU inference.

Loading a multimodal embedding model works exactly like loading a text-only model:

Some models might require a revision argument for now if the integration pull requests for the model is still pending. Once they're merged, you'll be able to load them without specifying a revision, like above.

The model automatically detects which modalities it supports, so there's nothing extra to configure. See Processor and Model kwargs if you want to control things like image resolution or model precision.

With a multimodal model loaded, model.encode() accepts images alongside text. Images can be provided as URLs, local file paths, or PIL Image objects (see Supported Input Types for all accepted formats):

You can compute similarities between text embeddings and image embeddings, since the model maps both into the same space:

As expected, "A green car parked in front of a yellow building" is most similar to the car image (0.51), and "A bee on a pink flower" is most similar to the bee image (0.67). The hard negatives ("A red car driving on a highway", "A wasp on a wooden table") correctly receive lower scores.

You might notice that even the best matching scores (0.51, 0.67) aren't very close to 1.0. This is due to the modality gap: embeddings from different modalities tend to cluster in separate regions of the space. Cross-modal similarities are typically lower than within-modal ones (e.g., text-to-text), but the relative ordering is preserved, so retrieval still works well.

For retrieval tasks, encode_query() and encode_document() are the recommended methods. Many retrieval models prepend different instruction prompts depending on whether the input is a query or a document, similar to how chat models might apply different system prompts depending on the goal. Model authors can specify their prompts in the model config, and encode_query() / encode_document() automatically load and apply the correct one:

Under the hood, both are thin wrappers around encode(), they just handle prompt selection for you. Here's what cross-modal retrieval looks like:

These methods accept the same input types as encode() (images, URLs, multimodal dicts, etc.) and pass through the same parameters. For models without specialized query/document prompts, they behave identically to encode().

Multimodal reranker (CrossEncoder) models score the relevance between pairs of inputs, where each element can be text, an image, audio, video, or a combination. They tend to outperform embedding models in terms of quality, but are slower since they process each pair individually. The currently available pretrained multimodal rerankers focus on text and image inputs, but the architecture supports any modality that the underlying model can handle.

The rank() method scores and ranks a list of documents against a query, supporting mixed modalities:

The reranker correctly identifies the car image (document 0) as the most relevant result, followed by the combined text+image document about a car in a European city (document 3). The bee image (document 1) scores lowest. Keep in mind that the modality gap can influence absolute scores: text-image pair scores may occupy a different range than text-text or image-image pair scores.

You can also check which modalities a reranker supports using modalities and supports(), just like with embedding models:

You can also use predict() to get raw relevance scores for specific pairs of inputs:

A common pattern is to use an embedding model for fast initial retrieval, then refine the top results with a reranker:

Since the corpus embeddings are pre-computed, the initial retrieval is fast even over millions of documents. The reranker then provides more accurate scoring over the smaller candidate set.

Multimodal models accept a variety of input formats. Here's a summary of what you can pass to model.encode():

You can check which modalities a model supports using the modalities property and supports() method:

The "message" modality indicates that the model accepts chat-style message inputs with interleaved content. In practice, you rarely need to use this directly. When you pass strings, URLs, or multimodal dicts, the model converts them to the appropriate message format internally. Sentence Transformers supports two message formats:

The format is auto-detected from the model's chat template.

Since all inputs get converted into the same message format internally, you can mix input types in a single encode() call:

If a model doesn't follow either format and you need full control, you can pass raw message dicts with role and content keys directly:

This bypasses the automatic format conversion and passes the messages directly to the processor's apply_chat_template().

You may want to control image resolution bounds or model precision. Use processor_kwargs and model_kwargs when loading the model:

See the SentenceTransformer API Reference documentation for more details on these kwargs.

In Sentence Transformers v5.4, tokenizer_kwargs has been renamed to processor_kwargs to reflect that multimodal models use processors rather than just tokenizers. The old name is still accepted but deprecated.

Here are the multimodal models supported in v5.4, also available in the v5.4 integrations collection:

The older CLIP models continue to be supported:

These simple CLIP models still work well on lower-resource hardware.

To learn how to finetune these multimodal models on your own data, see the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

#10287. Google launches Intelligent Eyewear glasses: $395+, pre-order today, ships Dec. 10

After years of development, Google is launching its second foray into smart glasses with Intelligent Eyewear that supports Android and iOS. Pre-orders start today at Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, with the audio glasses shipping on December 10.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is meant to be worn all day rather than the sunglasses-heavy approach taken by others. The frames are 40-44 grams with the weight balanced evenly.

There is a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera for photos and videos (3K 30FPS or 1080p). You get image stabilization and HDR processing, while four microphones work to provide spatial audio capture. Google is also quite proud of its noise cancellation work.

There are two open-ear speakers for balanced audio and clear vocals. Control is done by a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes, or via voice commands, with Google debuting a new “Hey Gemini” hotword.

Another way to control Intelligent Eyewear is through your Pixel Watch or Galaxy Watch, with Fitbit Air support coming next year:

Notably, Gemini commands that invoke the camera — like visual search or translation — will not save images or videos to your Gemini History. These visuals won’t be used to train AI models or for ad targeting. Additionally, the glasses will “automatically redact bystanders’ faces from these visuals before Gemini processes them.”

Battery life (245mAh) is rated at nine hours on a single charge, with a fully topped-up charging case (Gentle Monster’s shown below) offering seven full charges. Power is transferred via contact pins located on the underside of the nose bridge.

Android XR runs on the Qualcomm Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 with 2GB of RAM and 64GB of storage. Other specifications include Bluetooth 5.4, Wi-Fi 6E, and IPX4 water resistance. Samsung is responsible for engineering the hardware, while there are two eyewear brands at launch.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three styles and a total of 14 variations. Alden, Reid, and Wren are inspired by the brand’s “most beloved silhouettes.” Pricing starts at $395 for optical and sun styles in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black.

The Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear collection features six frames in bold colors like dark red, pink, gray, and yellow, with 16 total variations. They can be paired with tinted, clear, blue, or brown lenses, with prescription options available for most designs. Pricing starts at $449 and will be available in the US and South Korea.

Intelligent Eyewear can be used for contextual visual searches, asking Gemini about your day, and having it accomplish tasks.

Google Maps offers turn-by-turn directions, while there’s real-time Google Translate in over 70 languages.

Like on phones, Gemini Guided Vision “offers conversational audio descriptions to people with vision impairments.” This can be used to read fine print, identify color differences, find items, and explore unfamiliar places.

These glasses also serve as always-available headphones with support for YouTube Music, Spotify, Apple Music, and Audible. The Glasses companion app supports:

Pre-orders for Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear start today with retail availability on December 10.

Nvidia Board Director Mark Stevens sold about 4.2 million of his shares, netting him around $1 billion in cash, almost exactly two months before Jensen Huang was accused of having “close ties” to an alleged Chinese spy. According to Moneywise.com, Stevens started the sale from August 31 to September 2, when Nvidia stock hovered between $220 and $226, which made him $411 million. The next tranche, totaling $236 million, came in the next couple of days as Nvidia traded from $227 to $234. The final sale happened on September 18 at around $220 per share, making Stevens approximately $300 million. These three transactions would have made him somewhere around $947 million.

Last year, Jensen Huang sold up to six million Nvidia shares, netting him around $925 million. However, unlike Stevens, who had no plan, this move was announced six months earlier in a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan to help avoid accusations of insider trading.

Nvidia’s stock price has taken a beating since the scandal broke, with the company trading at $162.85 at the time of writing, its lowest level in the past 12 months. When the story first broke at the end of October, Nvidia shares were at around $205. It then started sliding, with the price at $178.67 after Jensen admitted to the affair last Sunday, although he did not name the involved party.

A second affair was revealed a few days after the former Nvidia chief’s confession, leading to his resignation from the company a few hours after that. The news sent Nvidia stock down to $151.09 — a nearly 25% drop from before the scandal. It recovered somewhat after the initial shock, climbing to nearly $170 before Friday’s trading, but took a beating again soon after the market opened.

Despite the sale, Stevens still holds about 27.5 million Nvidia shares, making him the second-largest shareholder after Jensen and Lori Huang. The price difference between today and September 18 is around $57, meaning he would have lost 25% of the value if he had sold after the scandal broke. Furthermore, his remaining Nvidia shares have lost more than $1.5 billion in value in just one quarter. Still, selling one’s holdings in a company as a board director does not constitute a crime. After all, it's unlikely that one could have predicted how hard Jensen Huang would fall in such a short time.

#10285. Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

While I acknowledge Meta’s role in bringing smart glasses to a mainstream audience, it has proven to be an irresponsible steward. Its “growth at all costs” mindset has actively poisoned people’s perception of the form factor. Under Meta’s watch, glasses have gained a creepy connotation before their utility has been fully realized.

Google’s second take on smart glasses is the exact opposite of what Meta has done. Every single aspect has been considered, and the result is worthy of being most people’s introduction to the form factor.

Officially, Android XR glasses are known as Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear. The branding is a mouthful, and I’m not quite sure “Intelligent Eyewear” will take off. Something more colloquial, like “Google glasses” — glasses.google is the landing page — or “Samsung glasses,” will probably stick in the public consciousness.

That critique aside, the name reflects how Google wants Intelligent Eyewear to actually replace your existing glasses. Unlike the Ray-Ban trap that I frankly think Meta did not consider, Google’s offerings are not situational or activity-based devices like sunglasses. These are a “smart” upgrade to the assistive device some people have to wear.

As a wearable, smart glasses are a bit like smartwatches in that the platonic design is pretty well established and indistinguishable from traditional eyewear. Unlike watches, glasses are so visible on people’s faces that form overrides everything else.

Fortunately, the Samsung hardware I wore for an hour last week looks and feels like glasses, almost unremarkably so. I’d venture to say that audio-only glasses without a display are a solved design challenge. Google emphasized that, at 41 grams, this is the lightest pair of smart glasses on the market, and it worked to make sure the weight is distributed evenly.

The sides of the stems that face your head feature translucent plastic that lets you see the internal components. I liked that small design choice. You can control the glasses using voice commands, with Google debuting a new “Hey Gemini” hotword for the form factor. While “Hey Google” and “OK Google” remain available, the new one is meant to reflect how big a role Gemini plays on smart glasses.

There is also a touchpad on the right stem that accepts taps and swipes, while a button up top lets you take pictures and record video. Another way you’ll be able to control the glasses is with your Pixel Watch and Galaxy Watch. You can play/pause audio and enable Gemini using double-pinch and wrist gestures. Notably, gesture support is also coming to the Fitbit Air next year.

From its internal testing, Google tells me that which input method people use is pretty situational and ends up being natural. At the beginning of my demo, I favored the touchpad, but by the end, I was leaning toward voice commands.

Talking to Intelligent Eyewear uses Gemini Live. Some prompts, like take a picture or play a song, are one-shot “chat” commands in phone parlance, but for the most part, you’re using Gemini’s back-and-forth conversation mode. Google heavily customized the Gemini Live model for glasses to reduce latency, shorten responses, and tightly integrate the camera.

Even compared to my last demo in May, the latency of voice commands has come a long way. That said, I need more time to see if it’s really fast enough to use as a primary interaction method for most commands.

Similarly, Google will blur all faces and filter out bystander voices before it gets uploaded to Gemini in the cloud. This on-device processing occurs on your phone.

Since that visual media isn’t being saved, the external indicator light won’t be active when you’re talking to Gemini. The LED is only on when photos or videos are being saved and can be reviewed later.

That indicator light features anti-tamper detection that prevents recording. Algorithms detect whether the LED is covered by stickers or markers, with this process featuring hardware verification when the glasses are in their charging case.

Google’s “Glasses” companion app, with Samsung having a near-identical version for Galaxy phones, is pretty similar to the version for Pixel Watch. Unlike the bloated “Meta AI” app, it’s just for settings rather than the very definition of a growth hack with a full chatbot. The difference is staggering, and something Google deserves a bit of credit for in this age of throwing AI into every crevice of day-to-day smartphone usage.

Under the hood, the glasses are offloading a lot of processing to your phone. This includes HDR pipelines and video stabilization. The 12MP camera takes pictures in a 4:3 aspect ratio, while you can record up to 90 seconds of video. Images are transferred immediately to your phone over Wi-Fi, while videos wait until the glasses are charging to preserve battery life. I am so excited by point-of-view photography and the instantaneous capture the glasses offer, and early impressions of camera quality are positive.

Another thing I want to test is how Intelligent Eyewear fares as always-available headphones. There are two open-ear speakers and four microphones, and Google is clearly very proud of the noise-cancellation work in place.

As someone who has been waiting for smart glasses since 2012, I cannot overstate my annoyance at how Meta allowed smart glasses to gain a scummy undertone, if not overtone. It should have been more proactive to societal issues. Meanwhile, Meta releasing glasses without a camera, thus removing the primary utility of real-world context, makes me deeply question its belief that this is the future.

Smart glasses that know what you’re interacting with in the world can be extremely useful. That always-available camera is a genuine physical advantage over smartphones. It unlocks new use cases and convenience that are just not possible with something that goes in your pocket.

Google took a long time to get back to glasses. From what I’ve used so far, the wait will be worth it. The hardware and designs are solid, while the software is chock-full of innovative, well-considered ideas.

#10284. Waypoint-1.5: Higher-Fidelity Interactive Worlds for Everyday GPUs

Waypoint-1.5 is Overworld’s next real-time video world model, built to bring interactive generative worlds to the hardware people actually own.

The first release of Waypoint showed that real-time generative worlds were possible. It proved that interactive world models could be more than passive video demos, and that locally runnable systems could begin to close the gap between generating a world and actually stepping into one.

Waypoint-1.5 builds directly on that foundation. This release improves visual fidelity, expands the range of hardware that can run the model locally, and takes another step toward interactive world simulation without datacenter-scale compute.

On desktop hardware including RTX 3090 through 5090, Waypoint-1.5 can generate real-time environments at up to 720p and 60 FPS. This release also introduces a 360p tier designed to run smoothly across a much broader range of consumer hardware, including gaming laptops, and (soon) Apple Silicon Macs.

The biggest change in Waypoint-1.5 is accessibility.

With Waypoint-1, we proved the core experience. With Waypoint-1.5, we wanted to make that experience available on more machines without giving up real-time interactivity. That meant building two model tiers: a 720p model for higher-performance hardware, and a 360p model optimized for broader deployment.

We also scaled training dramatically. Waypoint-1.5 was trained on nearly 100x more data than Waypoint-1, which significantly improves the model’s ability to generate more coherent environments and more consistent motion over time.

Under the hood, Waypoint-1.5 also incorporates more efficient video modeling techniques to reduce redundant computation across frames. That matters because real-time world models are not judged only by how a single frame looks. They are judged by whether the world responds instantly, stays coherent as you move through it, and remains usable on local hardware.

A lot of recent progress in generative video and world models has focused on visual fidelity. Those results matter, but fidelity alone is not what makes an interactive world feel real.

What people remember is responsiveness. They remember whether the environment reacts to them, whether motion stays coherent, whether the world holds together as they explore it, and whether the whole experience feels immediate instead of delayed.

That is the gap we care about most: the difference between watching a generated scene and actually being inside one.

If world models only run on large GPU clusters, they remain impressive demos. If they run locally on consumer hardware, they become something much more useful: a foundation for interactive entertainment, creative tooling, simulation, and AI-native environments people can actually explore.

Waypoint-1.5 is designed around that idea: not just better videos, but more responsive and explorable worlds that remain accessible on consumer hardware.

The first is local execution through Overworld Biome. This release is designed to run across a wide range of hardware configurations, and the updated Biome runtime makes local setup much simpler. With the new installer flow, users can go from download to running the model locally in minutes.

The second is Overworld Stream, which lets you try Waypoint-1.5 instantly in the browser with no local setup required.

Whether you want immediate access or full local control, Waypoint-1.5 is built to support both.

Additionally, we provide World Engine, our flexible, easy to use, core inference library powering our official clients, along with nearly a dozen third party clients and libraries.

Waypoint started with a simple question: what would it take for generative worlds to become truly interactive?

Early generative systems showed that models could produce convincing images and videos. But building environments that people can explore, control, and interact with in real time is a different challenge entirely.

Waypoint-1.5 is another step in that direction, improving fidelity and expanding hardware accessibility while continuing to push real-time interactive generation onto local machines.

We think the future of world models will not be defined only by what they can render, but by whether people can actually inhabit and interact with them in real time.

Download Waypoint-1.5, run it locally with Biome, or jump in instantly on Overworld.stream.

And if you build something fun, strange, or unexpectedly immersive with it, we’d love to see it.

The Pentagon has been testing packs of autonomous ground vehicles (UGVs) in simulated combat situations. In mid-October, at Fort Knox’s St. Vith Range in Kentucky, four UGVs “worked as a team, negotiating and surveilling the rolling landscape in search of enemy forces,” recalls a DARPA blog post. These UGVs are highly modular and can be kitted out with a wide range of tactical add-ons, but target engagement was controlled by a human operator. This latest exercise was prompted by the request of European allies.

“Out here at Fort Knox, we’re looking at how autonomous mobility technology can be paired with payloads to enable new warfighter capabilities,” explained Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA. The blog notes that this location was also chosen as it represents a similar landscape to the European theater.

During the demo an operator received a tip about a simulated threat alongside some satellite imagery. They then sent the pack of UGVs to the area to surveil the landscape and identify targets. Smartly, a sole UGV went ahead of the pack to scout, with the three others waiting behind. The scout UGV was equipped with a flying drone. In a real-world scenario this could have been flown for better visuals or to strike the targets from the sky. “Soldiers can mount anything and everything onto – 240 Bravos, drones, rockets,” said a technician attending the demo, as they are “super modular platforms.” The blog says three of the four UGVs in the exercise had drones.

After the designated area was scouted by the leading autonomous ground vehicle, other UGVs followed on “to provide cover and support.” A simulated rocket was fired at a target identified about 300 yards from the robot pack. Finally, the last robot came out of cover, higher up over a ridge, to assess the field of conflict.

It was emphasized that during the exercise, a human operator was controlling any kinetic engagement. “All the mobility, all the movement, all the detections, all of that is autonomous,” explained Gregory. “But they don’t pull the trigger until a human says pull the trigger.”

This exercise was part of DARPA’s Robotic Autonomy in Complex Environments with Resiliency, or RACER program. Expertise required for RACER’s success includes vehicle design, algorithm technologies, super intelligence, and secure communications.

After five years of work, these UGVs can now be instructed to complete tasks on the battlefield, instead of being manually driven, notes Gregory. They roam off-road as fast as any human driver could manage, at a minimum.

An app engineer has showcased his homemade breadboard 486 DX2 PC running Doom. The intricate explosion-of-wires system build appears to have taken just 16 days, with the first appearance of the legendary Intel CPU on @nagakurage’s timeline on October 24, and a video demo of some fragging in Doom published on November 9. Moreover, the Tokyo-based app engineer behind the project also developed and made a bezelicious ‘CRT monitor’ to go with the homemade early-90s-era gaming beast.

This project’s first signs of life were seen towards the end of October. On October 24, @nagakurage showcased the legendary Intel i486 DX2 CPU that he had acquired. It was the sought-after DX2 66 model, which meant it ran at a blistering 66 MHz internally, and 33 MHz externally (2x multiplier). On the other side of this gray made-in-Malaysia chip, you can see its 168 pins, which look incredibly tree-trunk-like by today’s standards.

The enthusiast next bought a Colorlight i9 v7.2 FPGA board to attach the CPU to and to cover chipset duties. We know this is a breadboard PC, but there are limits… Every pin of the 486 CPU appears to have been connected separately to an experimental ‘socket’ made using a baseboard.

RAM was added on October 31, and tweaked to be error-free. Then, on November 3, the enthusiast managed to add microSD storage to the system. That same day @nagakurage enjoyed seeing the breadboard 486 boot FreeDOS 1.3 for the first time [machine translation].

The app developer then took a 3D printing diversion and used his Bambu Lab A1 mini to output the parts necessary for a custom CRT-style enclosure. This was designed by Claude and was assembled with a 5-inch 800×480 Elecrow Raspberry Pi panel inside.

Finally, on November 9, @nagakurage showcased his breadboard PC and era-matching design beige-shelled monitor side-by-side and powered up. The seminal shooter looked smooth enough on the vintage 1992 silicon, as it should do.

Going forward, the enthusiast wants to refine this breadboard-based project and make it fully PC-98 compatible, in line with the dominant NEC PC-9800 series in Japan in the early 90s.

#10280. Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec

For most of the last decade, an API call looked like a transaction. A client sent a request, waited, and got a complete response back in one piece. That model is exactly what most API management tooling — including API Gateway — was built to handle, and it still describes a huge amount of production traffic.

But that no longer describes all traffic types. A model generating a response emits tokens as it produces them, not in one batch at the end. An agent working through a multi-step task reports progress as it goes. A dashboard, a collaborative editor, a live inference endpoint — these all need a connection that stays open and carries data in both directions.

Until now, developers building those experiences in API Gateway had to make an uncomfortable choice: put API Gateway in front of their APIs and give up streaming, or route streaming endpoints around the gateway and give up the authentication, API key enforcement, and observability that made the gateway essential in the first place. Teams ended up with a split estate — governed APIs on one path, ungoverned streaming traffic on another.

We're announcing that streaming support in API Gateway is available in Public Preview. Your streaming endpoints can now sit behind the same gateway, with the same policies, as everything else you serve.

For AI applications, streaming also strengthens API Gateway's connection to Gemini platform. A gateway that uses model routing now streams responses from Gemini, Claude and OpenAI gpt-oss models in model garden in Gemini platform as they're generated, and streaming backends you host anywhere else work the same way. Alongside Apigee and Agent Gateway in Gemini platform, API Gateway is the lightweight entry point to Google Cloud's AI gateway capabilities.

API Gateway now supports the full range of streaming patterns modern APIs rely on:

Streams can stay open for up to one hour. As with any long-lived connection, clients should implement reconnection logic so that a session survives the end of a stream — a well-behaved WebSocket or SSE client should be doing this anyway.

This is the part we are most pleased with: there is nothing new to learn.

Streaming is not a different product, a different resource type, or a different way of describing your API. There are no new extensions to add, no streaming-specific annotations, no separate spec for streaming operations. The same document that describes your existing API describes your streaming API.

Everything you already rely on continues to work exactly as before:

During Public Preview, you opt-in when creating the gateway:

That single flag is the entire difference. At GA, it is planned that streaming will simply be how API Gateway behaves, with no opt-in required and, as during Preview, no changes to your API config.

Alongside streaming, gateways get a deterministic default hostname:

Previously the default gateway.dev hostname included a generated hash, which meant you could not know your gateway's URL until after you had created it. That is a small thing that causes a lot of friction: you can't write the endpoint into a client config, a Terraform module, a CI pipeline, a firewall allowlist, or a partner integration doc until the resource exists — and if you tear the environment down and rebuild it, the URL changes underneath you.

Now the hostname is a pure function of values you already chose. You can generate it, template it, document it, and commit it to source control before the gateway exists, and you get the same URL every time you rebuild the same gateway in the same project and region. For anyone managing environments as code, or promoting a configuration from dev to staging to prod, this removes an entire category of bootstrapping problem.

Streaming isn't a niche feature for AI applications — it's the expected interaction pattern.

Users expect to see a model's response appear as it's generated, not after a thirty-second pause. Agents need to report intermediate steps. Tool-calling protocols and remote MCP servers depend on long-lived, incrementally-delivered connections. An API management layer that can't stream severely limits the user experience of AI applications.

With streaming, API Gateway becomes a viable front door for that agentic traffic — and the value of a front door is exactly the same as it's always been, only more urgent. AI endpoints are expensive, they consume quota, they need per-consumer authentication and rate limiting, and they need to be observable. These are the governance problems that an AI gateway is intended to solve. The alternative — every team standing up its own proxy in front of its own model endpoint — is how organizations end up unable to answer basic questions about who is calling what.

Model routing in API Gateway lets you expose a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint and dispatch requests to Gemini, Claude, or OpenAI gpt-oss models based on the model field in the request payload. Model routing plus streaming means clients get a familiar, standards-based streaming interface, while you retain centralized control over which models are reachable, by whom, and under what policy.

Streaming, model routing and MCP support are all features within API Gateway that provide a lightweight on-ramp to AI gateway capabilities within Google Cloud. These AI gateway capabilities allow teams to monitor, secure and control agentic traffic of tools, models and agents in their ecosystem, and they're delivered as a composable suite so you can choose the right gateway for each use case. For more expansive AI policies and full lifecycle management, use Apigee. To manage and secure agent connectivity, use Agent Gateway in Gemini platform. You can also combine these gateways: API Gateway or Apigee can sit in front of your agents and APIs, or behind Agent Gateway so your agents can reach models, tools, and MCP servers. For example, you can route your agent's egress through Agent Gateway for strict security governance, and then pass the request to API Gateway to handle model routing.

A few things to plan around while the feature is in Preview:

If you're already using API Gateway, the fastest way to see this working is to point a new streaming-enabled gateway at an existing backend that emits SSE and watch the events arrive incrementally. No spec changes needed.

#10279. ‘Hey Gemini’ hotword debuts on Android XR glasses

Google is finally introducing a “Hey Gemini” hotword for its AI assistant, but it’s only on Android XR glasses to start.

Around a decade after “Hey Google” made its debut, Google is introducing its first new always-listening hotword. “Hey Gemini” makes its debut on Google’s Intelligent Eyewear glasses powered by Android XR, with wearers able to use that hotword in place of “Hey Google.”

This is a move that doesn’t come as a huge surprise. If anything, it’s perhaps a bit overdue.

The move from Assistant to Gemini would have been the expected place for Google to make this change, but it’s one that many will certainly welcome. While the hotword you use really won’t matter much at the end of the day, “Hey Google” has been recognized by many to not roll of the tongue very nicely. It’s a phrase that’s easy to stumble over, where “Hey Gemini” is a bit smoother.

As for whether or not “Hey Gemini” will become the default on future product remains unclear, but it’s a change only available on glasses for now.

We’ve asked Google if both hotwords will be active on Android XR glasses, but it was implied that this is, in fact, the case. When paired to Samsung glasses, “Hey Bixby” may also be in play, as Samsung’s voice assistant is supported on Intelligent Eyewear. Exact functionality, though, is something we’re still waiting for more clarity on.

#10278. Meet HoloTab by HCompany. Your AI browser companion.

We built one of the most powerful computer-use AIs in the world. And made it directly accessible from your browser. On March 31st, we released Holo3, our most advanced computer-use model to date.

Building something powerful is one thing; making it accessible and easy to use is another. We’re doing both.

HoloTab is a Chrome extension that navigates the web just like a person would. It automates tasks across any website with zero setup or technical skills required. You describe what you want, and the agent handles it directly inside your browser, navigating interfaces, filling fields, and making decisions the same way you would. The vision models, the action planning, the interface understanding, all of it is running underneath, working for you, and all you ever see is the result.

Some tasks are quick and forgettable, but others are long and repetitive, the kind that reliably eat up your afternoon. You might find yourself cross-referencing competitor pricing across twenty different e-commerce tabs to update a master spreadsheet, or filtering through a dozen job boards and company career pages to find new listings, painstakingly porting the details into a tracking doc to manage your applications.

That's where routines come in. You start a recording, and HoloTab captures what you do in your tab in real time while you click or narrate along the way, demonstrating what you're doing and why. Your screen and your actions give HoloTab everything it needs, enriching the routine with enough context to actually understand the goal.

Once the recording stops, a routine is generated. From then on, you can re-run your routine or schedule it whenever you need to, and HoloTab will handle the rest on its own.

Computer-use AI is going to change how people work, research, and get things done, both in their professional and personal lives, and that shift is already closer than most people realize. But it shouldn't require a technical background to access, and the benefits shouldn't accrue only to teams with engineers who know how to wire these systems together.

#10277. Automating Contract Signing in Node.js: Webhooks, Verification, and Storing Signed PDFs

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

The code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint says so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

The trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:

Most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF shows what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:

Since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

In the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

Non-planar 3D printing has mostly been experimental, but PancakeSlicer could finally make more people interested in trying it out and find more ways to improve it and use it practically.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Alpaca Engineering posted a YouTube video yesterday showcasing his self-hostable non-planar slicer. He explains that most non-planar 3D printing — printing across all three axes, rather than in 2D horizontal layers — demonstrations are usually for research purposes, for demonstration and experimentation, with no easy way for most 3D printer owners to try out non-planar 3D printing. His project, named PancakeSlicer, aims to fix this by making his non-planar slicing algorithm as easy to implement as existing slicing workflows, even improving upon it with 3D printer management features.

Alpaca Engineering explains that every few months, a non-planar 3D printing demonstration goes viral, but is rarely adopted practically by most 3D printer owners. Most non-planar experiments are for research, with half-abandoned GitHub projects. He further explains that non-planar isn’t widely adopted not because there aren’t any general-purpose non-planar slicers, but because it’s not accessible and easily implemented in a familiar workflow, with 3D printer owners spoiled by modern workflows and not needing to manually run G-code directly from an SD card.

Commercially available 3D printers are also not optimized for non-planar 3D printing. The challenge with printing at various angles is the clearance angle needed to bring a print head up and down without crashing into its own print. The slicer uses 3D models of various print heads from different 3D printer models to know how to slice the object to avoid collisions, thus having limited support; but Alpaca Engineering has listed a large number of supported 3D printers from Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality, Voron, and many others. The varying shapes of the print heads also mean different printers will have different capabilities, with some managing less angle and curvature than others.

Alpaca Engineering also has great animations and practical demonstrations of the different slicing algorithms in the slicer, including how the algorithm slices the object for non-planar printing. We highly suggest you watch the video if you’re interested, as his animations explain non-planar slicing intuitively.

One of the best features of this slicer is its self-hosting features. Users can host the slicer from a desktop, NAS, or a home server and access it with a web UI, allowing multiple users to send print jobs from any device. It also has 3D printer management features, applying different profiles to different printer brands, unifying the experience without hopping from one slicer to another to operate multiple 3D printers — this is even available to Bambu Lab users, replacing Bambu Studio and Bambu Connect in LAN-only mode. The slicer can also manage two slice jobs at the same time in case other users happen to be slicing at the same time.

While PancakeSlicer isn’t the first to implement self-hosted 3D printer management features, it certainly levels up his initial goal of making non-planar slicing as easy to access as most modern workflows. We hope to see how more people can experiment with non-planar 3D printing, contribute their findings, and rapidly improve upon it as a genuinely practical slicing method.

#10274. Inside VAKRA: Reasoning, Tool Use, and Failure Modes of Agents

VAKRA Dataset | LeaderBoard | Release Blog | GitHub | Submit to Leaderboard

We recently introduced VAKRA, a tool-grounded, executable benchmark for evaluating how well AI agents reason and act in enterprise-like environments.

Unlike traditional benchmarks that test isolated skills, VAKRA measures compositional reasoning across APIs and documents, using full execution traces to assess whether agents can reliably complete multi-step workflows.

VAKRA provides an executable environment where agents interact with over 8,000+ locally hosted APIs backed by real databases spanning 62 domains, along with domain-aligned document collections. Tasks can require 3-7 step reasoning chains that combine structured API interaction with unstructured retrieval under natural-language tool-use constraints.

As can be seen below, models perform poorly on VAKRA - in this blog, we include additional dataset details about the tasks in VAKRA and present an analysis of failure modes we observed on different tasks.

As shown below, the VAKRA benchmark comprises of four tasks, each testing a different set of capabilities.

Fig 1: Representative examples of each capability in the VAKRA benchmark

This capability includes 2,077 test instances across 54 domains, requiring the use of tools from the SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD collections (Elder et al., 2026). Compared to the setup in Elder et al., the tool universe in SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD is expanded through the inclusion of a larger number of domains. Each domain is restricted to one tool collection, and tasks involve chaining 1–12 tool calls to arrive at the final answer.

Fig 2: Data sample from SEL-BIRD collection

As shown above, each instance has an associated JSON data source from which the answer must be derived. The MCP servers supporting this task include a special tool, called get_data(tool_universe_id=id), which must be called at the beginning of each instance. This tool initializes the data source, returns a lightweight preview of the data (see below Figure 3), and stores the full dataset server-side to avoid large data transfers. This prevents the inefficient transfer of large data over the MCP protocol. The call also configures the MCP server to expose the appropriate tool set based on the tool_universe_id and aligns the data source with the domain-specific database for the instance.

The SLOT-BIRD collection provides a global set of 7 tools for generic data manipulation (e.g., filtering, sorting), inspired by systems like Tableau and Google Analytics. The SEL-BIRD collection extends this by introducing more specialized tools: some are shared with SLOT-BIRD, while others are derived by flattening categorical arguments into separate functions (e.g., sort_data with argument ascending: bool = False becomes sort_data_ascending and sort_data_descending). Additionally, the generic (retrieve_data) function from SLOT-BIRD is replaced with query-specific getters. Every key in the data for a given instance has an associated get function (get_KEY_NAME) for an average of 4 get functions per instance.

Fig 3: Data preview obtained from `get_data` function

This capability includes 1,597 instances across 17 domains, requiring tools from an expanded REST-BIRD collection (Elder et al.). These use endpoint-style interfaces that provide highly specific, query-aligned endpoints that encapsulate most computation. They are served as REST APIs running in a FastAPI server, which is wrapped by the MCP server. This task requires selecting the correct APIs from the domain-specific tool set (as shown in the example in Figure 1). Each domain contains a minimum of 6 to a maximum of 328 tools (with an average of 116 tools). Similar to the previous task, the get_data tool configures the MCP server to expose only the relevant domain-specific APIs.

The OpenAI API Specification restricts the tool list input to a maximum length of 128 tools. This restriction requires an agent builder using this API to manage the length of the tool list directly via a shortlisting mechanism. In the baseline agents in our repository, a simple shortlisting capability handles this challenge.

The Capability 3 segment of the benchmark has 869 test instances drawn from 38 subject domains. These instances rely again on the REST-BIRD API collection, but add multi-hop reasoning to the challenge (refer to example in Figure 1). Multi-hop questions require multiple pieces of supporting evidence to be extracted and combined to reach an answer. The instances in this section require between one and five logical hops to answer a query. The question types distribution for queries within the test dataset is shown below in Figure 4.

Fig 4: API Hop-Type distribution for Capability 3 (MultiHop) and Hybrid Hop-Type distribution for Capability 4 (MultiHop MultiSource Reasoning)

Capability 4 includes 644 instances across 41 domains and is also built on the REST-BIRD API collection. Figure 4 above shows a distribution of hybrid hops for test queries without policies. It contains the most complex queries with the following characteristics:

Multi-Source: This segment adds document indices per domain. Queries in this capability could require information from these document indexes as well as API calls. Similar to Capability 3, this task also has Multi-Hop queries. The required information source applies at the per-hop level, so, for example, a question may entail three logical hops with sources: API - RAG (Document Retrieval) - API. To enforce correct reasoning, sources are decontaminated during data generation, i.e. information required for a given hop is available in only one source. For example, if a hop is to be answered using APIs, the document index is built by removing documents that likely contain the information needed to answer the question.

Multi-Turn: This segment of the dataset also adds multi-turn conversations to the setting. Each instance is a dialog with multiple turns. The data is released as context-response pairs, where the context encodes the current dialog history and the agent is only responsible for answering the current turn.

Tool-usage Policies: A subset of these instances includes tool-use policies that the agent is required to follow. These policies take the form of plain-text instructions about the knowledge sources that the agent is allowed to access and under which circumstances. For example:

The baseline agent in the project repo imposes adherence to these policies through a simple addition to the prompt: "You are a helpful assistant with access to tools.\n Tool Usage Constraint: {additional_instructions}.". Of course, agent builders are free to choose any constraint enforcement mechanism.

VAKRA evaluates agents in tool environments where success depends on both the ability to execute coherent, multi-step workflows and answer correctness. We introduce an execution-centric evaluation framework that assesses not only final outputs but also the full tool-execution trajectory that includes tool calls, inputs, and intermediate results.

The VAKRA Evaluator operates over two key inputs for each sample: a predicted final response and the corresponding tool-call trajectory. The tool calls from the predicted trajectory are executed in the same environment as the ground truth to verify intermediate tool outputs.

The evaluation follows a waterfall-style pipeline (Figure 6), where later stages are conditioned on earlier success:

Fig 6: Waterfall-style Evaluation Pipeline

Tool-Sequence Comparison Due to the presence of an executable environment, agents can explore the environment and sometimes return the answer by invoking a different set of APIs than the ones identified by us. In order to support alternative but valid tool invocations and reasoning paths, correctness is assessed by executing each predicted tool and comparing the set of tool responses against those from the ground truth (rather than enforcing strict step-level matching).

Specifically, we first perform a programmatic check, verifying whether all information present in the ground-truth tool responses is recovered by the predicted tool responses. This check may be inconclusive in cases involving partial matches, semantic equivalence, or differences in representation (e.g., ordering, aggregation, or formatting). In such cases, we apply a secondary LLM-based evaluation, adapted from the CRAG framework Yang et al., 2024, to determine whether the predicted trajectory retrieves all required information despite structural differences. This step uses an adapted prompt to determine whether the predicted trajectory captures all required information, even if obtained through a different sequence of tool calls.

Final Response Evaluation For trajectories that pass the previous check, the final response is evaluated using an LLM-based judge. This step ensures that the response is (i) grounded in the predicted tool outputs, and (ii) factually consistent with the ground truth answer, accounting for potential variations in phrasing or structure.

This design ensures that agents are rewarded not only for producing correct answers, but for obtaining them through valid and complete reasoning processes.

Every capability is equally weighted to obtain a final leaderboard score

To obtain a capability score, every sample within a capability is equally weighted for capabilities 1 through 3.

For capability 4, we weight heterogeneous queries higher:

We now present detailed error analysis across the four VAKRA capabilities. To facilitate our analysis, we adopt stage-wise error categorization to assign each failure to the first point of breakdown. Specifically, we evaluate, in order: (i) whether the correct tool(s) were selected, (ii) whether the required arguments were provided without omissions or hallucinations, (iii) whether argument values were correct, and (iv) whether the final response is both accurate and grounded in the tool outputs.

Since a single sample may exhibit multiple errors across different steps, we sequentially classify each instance to the earliest failing stage (e.g., tool selection errors take precedence over argument errors). This avoids double-counting and allows error categories to be interpreted as disjoint fractions of the dataset. While more granular metrics (e.g., precision/recall over tool usage) are possible (Elder et al., 2026), we find this formulation provides a simple and interpretable breakdown of agent failures.

The instances in this part of the benchmark required selecting and sequencing multiple tools to solve a single task. We have 2077 samples in this capability. This was challenging for all models, but GPT-OSS-120B performed best on this segment of the benchmark.

Fig 7: SEL-BIRD vs SLOT-BIRD Error Types Analysis

The Business Intelligence (BI) API capability contains two sets of APIs, from the SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD tool collections. The SEL part of this benchmark had 600 samples, while the SLOT part of the benchmark had 1477 samples. These two collections are grouped under the BI API capability, but have slightly different characteristics. The SLOT-BIRD collection has a smaller number of generic tools with a large number of parameter values to fill, while the SEL-BIRD collection has a larger set of tools and fewer parameters per tool. This focus is reflected in the relative errors made by models using these two tool collections.

Fig 8: Comparison of Accuracy Across Models by Hop Depth

Multi-hop reasoning increases the difficulty of the original task by requiring models to successfully answer multiple implicitly coupled questions, each of which requires selecting and calling the correct API. As expected, all models performed best on the questions with only a single logical hop, and saw performance degradations on 2-hop and again on 3+ hop questions.

Fig 9: Model Accuracy Rates by Interaction Type (API, Document-Retriever, Hybrid)

The final segment of the dataset includes document sources in addition to the tool/API sources in the other segments. This leads to instances that require single or multiple API calls, single or multiple document searches, or some combination of API calls and document searches.

Fig 10: Model Accuracy Rates by Policy Type

Policies introduce an additional layer of difficulty on top of multi-hop, multi-source reasoning. When policies align with the required source for answering i.e. they do not affect the tool list required for models to answer the question, we refer to it as "No Updates to Answer" -- as shown in Figure 10, all models except for Granite-4.0-h-Small-32B experience a clear drop in performance under policy constraints that restrict access to the most relevant information source (i.e. "Policy updates the answer").

In general, we find that models either violate constraints or fail to retrieve sufficient information, where they sometimes understood the policy but could not answer the question correctly, or they exhibit one of the previously analyzed failure modes.

Overall, tool-use policy-constrained settings suggest that while models can reason over tools and sources, they struggle to incorporate external constraints into that reasoning - often a key requirement for reliable real-world deployment.

VAKRA exposes a critical gap between surface-level tool competence and robust, end‑to‑end agent reliability. Although modern models can increasingly select APIs and execute isolated tool calls, VAKRA shows that these abilities alone are insufficient for real‑world deployment. In practice, models often break down when required to perform compositional reasoning under execution constraints—spanning APIs, documents, dialog context, and policy requirements.

Think your agent is solid? Put it to the test.

Run it on VAKRA and see where it falls apart—tool selection, multi-hop reasoning, or policy constraints.
