#10255. 10 Best AI App Builders I've Used in 2026 (and What Each One Gets Wrong)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free plan is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every plan, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

Bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web plans run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

v0's Free plan gives new users $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Figma's Starter plan is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human users.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

The caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

The CS 737X CDU (v2) brings an authentic, premium-build Boeing 737 Control Display Unit to the home cockpit, but its high price makes it a niche product for serious flight sim enthusiasts.

Accurate 1:1 replica of the real Boeing 737 Control Display Unit

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Thanks to the popularity of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020, followed by Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, a growing number of companies have entered the flight simulation peripheral market — offering everything from budget-friendly products to high-end equipment designed for professional and home cockpits.

Cockpit-Master and Cockpit-Simulator were jointly founded in 2018 to develop and manufacture flight simulation equipment. In 2024, the company was split into two divisions, with Cockpit-Simulator focusing on more premium, professional-grade equipment.

Today, we are looking at the CS 737X CDU v2, a 1:1 replica of the Boeing 737 Control Display Unit (CDU). We will examine its build quality, how closely it replicates the real 737 CDU, and how well it integrates with Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024.

Before taking a look at the product itself, let’s first look at the real 737 Control Display Unit (CDU) and explain its functionality.

The CDU is the primary interface pilots use to interact with the aircraft’s Flight Management System (FMS). The FMS can be thought of as the aircraft’s “brain,” handling a wide range of navigation and performance-related tasks. Pilots use the CDU to enter and modify the flight plan, while the FMS calculates the lateral route and vertical profile of the flight. It also manages performance calculations, monitors fuel and flight progress, and provides guidance to the autopilot.

The CDU features a display screen with six line select keys on either side. These keys allow pilots to select and enter information into specific fields on the display, including data entered into the scratchpad. The CDU also includes dedicated function keys for tasks such as accessing performance information and entering instrument departures and approaches. Below the display is an alphanumeric keypad, which pilots use to enter text and other data before transferring it to the selected field using the line select keys.

Unlike other consumer grade CDUs on the market, the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a full-metal, CNC-machined aluminum shell.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The buttons are made of silicone rubber, which also closely replicates what we felt in our time on a 737 simulator.

The display is where we noticed the biggest departure from the real 737 CDU. The real unit uses a thick, chemically strengthened, anti-glare optical glass cover, whereas the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a standard commercial display. As a result, there is some glare, although the display itself is excellent and offers very wide viewing angles. Despite this difference, the visual presentation is remarkably close to that of the real 737 CDU. The font styling, image sharpness, and color reproduction all closely match what you would see on the real flight deck.

The CS 737X CDU v2 also features a handle, which on the real aircraft is used for the maintenance crew to remove the CDU. This isn’t entirely necessary in a home setup, but it is a nice touch.

The unit can be easily placed on a desk using the included desktop stand, or integrated directly into a larger cockpit setup.

The weight, rigidity, and metallic construction closely replicate the feel of the CDU we experienced in a 737 simulator. The silicone buttons also require a firm, deliberate press to actuate, helping prevent accidental double-inputs during turbulence. This tactile resistance closely matches the experience of using the real unit. Manually entering a long route, rather than importing it from SimBrief, will give your fingers a workout – and will give you a newfound appreciation for the import button.

For our testing inside of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, we used the PMDG 737-800. We flew the following routes:

This allowed us to examine how the CS 737X CDU v2 handles routes of various duration.

For hardware, the device only requires a USB connection. It also requires the CockpitSimulator Bridge, which needs to be left open throughout the flight. This can be downloaded from the official Cockpit-Simulator site.

The overall feel of the unit, combined with the firm, deliberate key presses, adds another layer of immersion. More importantly, having a physical CDU means we can operate it directly — rather than panning the camera toward the virtual CDU, zooming in, and navigating it with a mouse. This makes interacting with the FMS considerably faster and more intuitive.

This is particularly useful when ATC gives you a direct-to instruction shortly after takeoff, while you are still hand-flying the aircraft. Performing the direct-to operation on a physical CDU is much easier than interacting with the virtual CDU, as it allows you to make the necessary inputs without taking your eyes away from the Primary Flight Display.

One of the first things that stood out was the extremely low input latency. Our key presses were reflected almost instantly on both the unit’s physical display and the virtual CDU inside Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, making the two feel effectively synchronized.

We were also able to switch seamlessly between the various CDU pages, even with longer flight plans loaded into the unit. Everything shown on the virtual CDU was accurately reproduced on the hardware, including aircraft-specific options for the PMDG 737-800 we were flying. The information was presented with accurate fonts, colors, and formatting, making the physical CDU feel like a natural extension of the one inside the simulator.

The CS 737X CDU v2 is the most premium and immersive Boeing 737 CDU we have tested. From the weight and feel of its metallic construction to the tactile resistance of the silicone keys and the accurate rendering of fonts and colors on the display, nearly every aspect of the unit contributes to an authentic experience. It's a fitting addition to any high-end home cockpit setup.

This level of construction and attention to detail comes at a price: the CS 737X CDU v2 retails for $799, which means it will likely be out of reach for many flight simmers. But if you're building a dedicated, high-end cockpit and looking for a CDU that closely replicates the experience of the real aircraft, it's an excellent addition.

#10252. How to Use Transformers.js in a Chrome Extension

We recently released a Transformers.js demo browser extension powered by Gemma 4 E2B to help users navigate the web.

While building it, we ran into several practical observations about Manifest V3 runtimes, model loading, and messaging that are worth sharing.

This guide is for developers who want to run local AI features in a Chrome extension with Transformers.js under Manifest V3 constraints.

By the end, you will have the same architecture used in this project: a background service worker that hosts models, a side panel chat UI, and a content script for page-level actions.

In this guide, we will recreate the core architecture of Transformers.js Gemma 4 Browser Assistant, using the published extension as a reference and the open-source codebase as the implementation map.

Before diving in, a quick scope note: I will not go deep on the React UI layer or Vite build configuration. The focus here is the high-level architecture decisions: what runs in each Chrome runtime and how those pieces are orchestrated.

If Manifest V3 is new to you, read this short overview first: What is Manifest V3?.

In MV3, your architecture starts in public/manifest.json. This project defines three entry points:

The background service worker also handles chrome.action.onClicked to open the side panel for the active tab. Related entry point to know: a popup can be defined with action.default_popup and works well for quick actions. This project uses a side panel for persistent chat, but the orchestration pattern is the same.

The key design decision is to keep heavy orchestration in the background and keep UI/page logic thin.

One practical consequence of this division is that the conversation history also lives in background (Agent.chatMessages): the UI sends events like AGENT_GENERATE_TEXT, background appends the message, runs inference, then emits MESSAGES_UPDATE back to the side panel.

This split avoids duplicate model loads, keeps the UI responsive, and respects Chrome's security boundaries around DOM access.

Once runtimes are separated, messaging becomes the backbone. In this project, all messages are typed through enums in src/shared/types.ts.

The orchestration rule is simple: the background is the single coordinator; side panel and content script are specialized workers that request actions and render results.

In src/shared/constants.ts, this extension uses two model roles:

The split is intentional: Gemma 4 handles reasoning/tool decisions, while MiniLM generates vector embeddings for the semantic similarity search in ask_website and find_history.

All inference runs in background (src/background/background.ts):

This gives a single model host for all tabs/sessions, avoids duplicate memory usage, and keeps the side panel UI responsive. Because models are loaded from the background service worker, artifacts are cached under the extension origin (chrome-extension://) rather than per-website origins, which gives one shared cache for the whole extension install.

MV3 lifecycle note: service workers can be suspended and restarted, so model runtime state should be treated as recoverable and re-initialized when needed.

Why keep this narrow: permissions define user trust and Chrome Web Store review risk. Request only what your features actually need, and state clearly that inference runs locally in the extension runtime so users understand where their data is processed.

Before the execution loop, it helps to understand how model tool calling works (the basis for any agentic workflow). You pass messages plus a tool schema (name, description, and parameters), and Transformers.js formats the actual prompt from those inputs using the model's chat template. Because chat templates are model-specific, the exact tool-call format depends on the model you use. With Gemma-4-style templates, the model emits a special tool-call token block when it decides to call one.

At generation time, the model can emit output like:

That is exactly why this project has a normalization layer (webMcp) and a parser (extractToolCalls): model output must be converted into deterministic tool executions.

src/background/agent/webMcp.tsx normalizes extension tools into a model-friendly shape:

Example tools include get_open_tabs, go_to_tab, open_url, close_tab, find_history, ask_website, and highlight_website_element.

The core design choice here is to separate internal model messages from UI-facing chat messages:

This keeps user communication clean while preserving a deterministic tool loop in the background.

State placement is another architectural decision that matters a lot in MV3. In this implementation, state is split by lifecycle and access pattern:

As described in section 1.2, keeping conversation history in background gives one canonical state across UI updates. This keeps short-lived state in memory, durable settings in extension storage, and heavy retrieval data in a local database.

You do not need a complex build setup, but MV3 does require predictable outputs for each runtime.

The goal is simple: one artifact per Chrome entry point, in the exact place public/manifest.json expects.

The architecture choice that unlocks this whole project is clear separation of concerns: background owns orchestration and model execution, UI surfaces stay thin, and content scripts handle page access.

This project uses a side panel, but the same approach works for other setups:

The practical rule is simple: decide where state lives (global, tabId, or site-scoped), keep that state and the model inference in background (basically as background services), and let UI/content runtimes act as focused clients.

Darrel Dai wants to know the exact reasons why Jensen resigned.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Just days after Jensen Huang suddenly resigned from his position at Nvidia, an Nvidia Robot Research Engineer said that he would leave the company as well. But more than just showing support for the former CEO with a generic “I stand with Jensen” message, Darrel Dai laid out several reasons for the decision on X.

I’ve decided to leave NVIDIA. There are a few things I want to say. As a robotics engineer at NVIDIA, I have seen Jensen as much more than the company’s CEO. I admire his willingness to invest in a future that was not yet obvious. He committed to CUDA long before the deep learning boom and positioned NVIDIA for AI before it became everyone’s priority. Those decisions helped build the infrastructure that powers today’s AI. I have seen that same vision in physical AI: investing in robotics, sharing open-source tools and projects, and building computing platforms that bring AI into the physical world. This is the work I do every day—and a future I believe in. But what matters most to me is the culture he helped build. Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly. In a company this large, that connection matters. It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard. That is why this has been so disappointing. I do not have all the facts surrounding the allegations, and I cannot prejudge the investigation. My admiration for Jensen does not put him above scrutiny. What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me. I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected. I understand that some information cannot be shared immediately. But that does not erase the feeling of being left outside a decision that affects the company we help build every day. A company’s greatness comes from its leadership, its governance, and the people who turn its ambitions into reality. Employees’ trust and sense of belonging are part of that, too. Jensen’s vision and the engineering culture he shaped were important reasons I wanted to stay. His departure led me to decide that my own chapter here should also come to a close. I leave with sadness and gratitude. The colleagues I have worked with, and the work we believed in together, will always matter to me. These are my personal views.November 15, 2026

“What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me,” the engineer posted. “I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected.”

It seems that Jensen Huang has gained the respect of the people working under him, with many calling for his reinstatement despite the many controversies he is currently facing. There’s also an online petition demanding that the Nvidia board “Bring Jensen Back,” with over 150,000 signatures at the time of writing.

Nvidia is centered around Jensen Huang, with the former chief executive reportedly having a small army of 60 people directly reporting to him. But despite his busy schedule and legendary persona, Dai said that “Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly,” and that “It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.” Dai also pointed out that “employees’ trust and sense of belonging” are part of what makes a company great. More importantly, Nvidia is known as one of the tech companies with the most generous pay packages. Jensen was even quoted saying, “I pay my employees as much as I can.”

It remains unclear what the former Nvidia CEO will do after all these issues. Elon Musk has already said on X that “it would be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang, especially as he’s embarking on his own ambitious chipmaking journey. As for the employees left behind at Nvidia, some are staying and have shown their full support to interim CEO Colette Kress, while many more want him back. However, there has also been talk that various Silicon Valley tech and semiconductor firms are aggressively attempting to poach Nvidians, although these are just rumors so far.

#10249. DeepSeek-V4: a million-token context that agents can actually use

DeepSeek released V4 today. Two MoE checkpoints are on the Hub: DeepSeek-V4-Pro at 1.6T total parameters with 49B active, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 284B total with 13B active. Both have a 1M-token context window. The benchmark numbers are competitive, but not SOTA. It doesn't matter. The real innovation is how DeepSeek v4 is designed for efficient large context length support, and hence as one of the best candidates for agentic tasks.

Focusing on long running agentic workloads. Running a frontier open model as an agent today breaks in predictable ways. The model stops. You reprompt. The trace blows past the context budget, or the KV cache fills the GPU, or tool-call round trips degrade halfway through a long task. V4 is built to fix these known failures, and point the way for the community to follow.

This post covers three things: what the architecture does differently to make long-context inference cheap, the agent-specific post-training decisions that compound on top of it, and some takeaways from the paper that help reason about these changes.

A 1M context window is just capacity, not performance. Whether you can use it depends on the cost of every forward pass at that depth. For an agent running a long tool-use trajectory (a SWE-bench task, a multi-step browse session, a terminal session with hundreds of commands), every tool result is appended to the context, and every subsequent token pays the full attention cost against everything that came before.

Two numbers matter: single-token inference FLOPs and KV cache size. Both grow with sequence length. At 1M tokens, DeepSeek-V4-Pro requires 27% of single-token inference FLOPs compared with DeepSeek-V3.2, so it runs faster on the same hardware. It also uses 10% of the KV cache memory. V4-Flash drops these numbers even further: 10% of the FLOPs and 7% of the KV cache.

If we compare the KV cache memory against a established architecture like grouped query attention with 8 heads, stored in the usual bfloat16 format, DeepSeek v4 requires roughly 2% the cache size. This makes it much easier to deploy for very large context handling.

Figure 1: benchmark comparison (left), per-token FLOPs and accumulated KV cache against sequence length (right).

The efficiency gain comes from splitting attention into two mechanisms and interleaving them across layers.

Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) compresses KV entries by 4x along the sequence dimension using softmax-gated pooling with a learned positional bias. A lightning indexer (FP4, ReLU-scored multi-head dot product) picks the top-k compressed blocks per query. It inherits the sparse-selection idea from DeepSeek Sparse Attention in V3.2, but runs it over blocks that are already 4x shorter than the original sequence. The indexer's search space shrinks with it.

Figure 3: CSA. The compressor collapses every 4 tokens into one compressed KV entry. The lightning indexer picks the top-k compressed blocks per query. A sliding-window branch handles the most recent uncompressed tokens.

Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) compresses KV entries by 128x and drops the sparse selection. Every query attends densely to every compressed block. The compressed sequence is short enough that dense attention is cheap.

Figure 4: HCA. A heavier compressor (128x vs. 4x) followed by dense attention over the compressed stream, with the same sliding-window branch for recency.

The layers alternate between CSA and HCA. Different layers carry different attention patterns, and forcing one mechanism across all of them wastes capacity. In V4-Pro's 61-layer stack, layers 0–1 are HCA, layers 2–60 alternate CSA and HCA, and the MTP block at the end runs sliding-window only.

Both paths use FP8 storage for most KV entries and BF16 only for the RoPE dimensions. The lightning indexer inside CSA runs in FP4. These storage choices compound with the compression ratios to produce the 2% KV cache figure.

Figure 2: overall architecture. Attention layers alternate between CSA and HCA. Feed-forward layers use DeepSeekMoE. Residual connections are replaced with manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC).

Efficient long-context attention is necessary for agent workflows but not sufficient. The paper describes three post-training and infrastructure choices that target agent use cases directly.

V3.2 kept reasoning traces across tool-result rounds but discarded them whenever a new user message arrived. For an agent handling a single user turn, this was fine. For multi-turn agentic workflows, where the user sends a follow-up after the agent has already chained several tool calls, the model lost its accumulated reasoning and had to reconstruct state.

V4 preserves reasoning content across user message boundaries when the conversation contains tool calls. The model retains the complete reasoning history across all rounds, including across user turns. This allows a coherent, cumulative chain of thought over long-horizon agent tasks. For conversational use without tools, the old behavior is preserved: reasoning is flushed on each turn to keep context concise.

Figure 7: thinking with tools (top) preserves reasoning across all turns. Thinking without tools (bottom) discards reasoning at each new user message.

V4 introduces a |DSML| special token and an XML-based tool-call format. The XML format reduces escaping failures compared to JSON-in-string tool calls, a common failure mode when models emit nested quoted content.

The schema separates string parameters (passed as-is with string="true") from structured parameters (passed as JSON with string="false"). This removes a class of parsing errors around numbers and booleans that JSON tool-call formats routinely hit.

The agent behavior was trained with RL against real tool environments. The paper describes the sandbox infrastructure built for that purpose. DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec) is a Rust platform that exposes four execution substrates behind one Python SDK: function calls, containers, microVMs (Firecracker), and full VMs (QEMU). A single cluster runs hundreds of thousands of concurrent sandboxes.

Three DSec features matter for agent training: fast image loading via layered 3FS storage (so RL rollouts do not wait on container startup), preemption-safe trajectory replay (so interrupted training steps resume without re-running tool calls), and a uniform API across substrates (so training harnesses target function calls or full VMs without rewriting). These infrastructure decisions underpin the agent benchmark scores.

The knowledge and reasoning numbers are competitive but not leading. The agent numbers are where V4-Pro-Max separates from the field.

Specific numbers from the agent section of Table 6:

In the paper's internal R&D coding benchmark, 30 curated tasks across PyTorch, CUDA, Rust, and C++, V4-Pro-Max hits 67% pass rate, versus 47% for Sonnet 4.5 and 70% for Opus 4.5. In a survey of 85 DeepSeek developers using V4-Pro as their daily driver, 52% said it was ready to replace their current primary coding model and 39% leaned toward yes.

The long-context retrieval numbers are in Figure 9. MRCR 8-needle accuracy stays above 0.82 through 256K tokens and holds at 0.59 at 1M.

Figure 9: MRCR 8-needle retrieval. V4-Pro-Max stays above 0.82 through 256K and holds at 0.59 at 1M.

Four checkpoints are on the Hub. The instruct models use FP4 for MoE expert weights and FP8 for everything else. The base models are FP8 throughout.

Both instruct models support three reasoning modes: Non-think (fast, no chain of thought), Think High (explicit reasoning in blocks), and Think Max (maximum reasoning effort with a dedicated system prompt). Think Max requires a context window of at least 384K tokens. The recommended sampling parameters across all modes are temperature=1.0, top_p=1.0.

The V4-Pro numbers on SWE Verified, MCPAtlas, and the internal R&D benchmark put it at parity with frontier closed models on agent tasks. The open question is how the community's tool harnesses adapt to the |DSML| schema and whether the interleaved thinking gains transfer to out-of-domain agent frameworks.

Figures in this blog post are from the technical report at DeepSeek_V4.pdf.

According to my personal tests DeepSeek V4 Flash (Non-thinking mode) passed the Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval test on both 32k and 435k actual prompt tokens with a 100% result across depths of 0-100%. In no-needle negative control with the NOT_FOUND instruction, the model also returned 100% correct failures, reducing the risk of contamination and false positives.

So thinking mode may degrade behaviour in some tests.

#10248. I’d rather use Android XR glasses over Meta Ray-Bans for the app alone

In trying out Google’s Intelligent Eyewear Android XR glasses for the first time, one of my main takeaways is that it’s the app, not necessarily the glasses themselves that would push me into using them over the mainstay Meta Ray-Bans.

One of the inherent advantages that Android XR glasses were always going to have over third-party options is native integration. It’s something we see frequently, and perhaps most well-known on smartwatches.

The “Glasses” app on Android/Pixel, iOS, and Samsung Galaxy devices is dead simple. While we can’t show you the full app just yet as the one we were able to try was not completely final, it’s a very simple experience.

The app opens to an overview of your glasses to show their connection and battery status, with settings below for Gemini, apps, the camera, and more. You’ll also be able to see things such as what the various lights on the glasses mean, tutorials, and more. There’s no bloat and no messing around – it’s a utility to just make adjustments or control the glasses as needed.

You’ll probably be using this app mostly to view the photos and videos captured on Android XR glasses. Google has this set up to auto-import photos in nearly real-time. It only takes about 4 seconds to import and the process starts immediately for photos. Videos, on the other hand, take longer and may need to be manually imported (for the sake of battery in part, Google mentioned).

Across the three main platforms, there are some differences. The iPhone app doesn’t import photos quite as fast, and Samsung has its own app to fit in with One UI’s design language for Galaxy users, but the core premise is the same across all three.

While we’ll have to see how this works in real life, I was blown away by how simple it all was, though that might be because the bar is below the floor.

Meta’s Ray-Bans (and newer Meta Glasses) dominate the smart glasses conversation, and I think that the app is one of the biggest problems. It’s certainly one of the biggest reasons I’ve barely touched my Wayfarers in recent months. That’s because, in early 2025, Meta replaced its dedicated “View” app for its glasses with a Meta AI app, which is just invasive and distasteful in my book. Meta is no stranger to shoving AI down the throat of its existing users. Another well-known move was converting Facebook and Instagram search into AI search boxes with creepy levels of context and invasive actions – it makes Google’s AI Overviews look tame by comparison. But I’d argue the most aggressive was this move with its glasses. Something as simple as tweaking a setting or importing a photo now forces you to dodge an AI chatbot.

Truly, Meta’s app is the worst, and I applaud Google for building a very simple utility for Android XR glasses instead.

#10246. This Quest 3 golf club actually improved my scores, but it comes at a cost

The AMVR GA2 is a fresh take on a Quest 3 golf club accessory, and I was pleasantly surprised with what it did for my scores.

In the past decade of covering VR devices and accessories, I’ve used a lot of golf clubs. Short clubs. Long clubs. Adjustable length clubs. Clubs with realistic weight. Even a club with a magnet inside that makes a convincing “thwack!” sound every time you swing it. But the AMVR GA2’s inclusion of a proper club head at the bottom does something fascinating for its physics, and I immediately noticed the difference at the end of the first course I played with this Quest 3 golf club.

Most VR golf club accessories, including the first-gen AMVR GA1, stick the controller at the bottom of the shaft where the head usually goes. This makes sense since you don’t hit a real ball with a VR golf club accessory; it’s all virtual. But, ironically, putting a proper golf club head on the end (and the controller in the middle of the shaft) apparently does make a difference. This one works with both the Meta Quest 3 and Quest 3S, but not the older Meta Quest 2 or Quest Pro.

I’m not going to delve into the physics of why this works, but it’s likely that shifting the fulcrum point improves it. I didn’t expect this at all. When AMVR told me about their new club, I accepted because the company typically makes top-notch accessories. I really didn’t need another club in my extensive Quest 3 golf club collection. But I’m glad I did, because I’ve done much better than usual in my weekly Walkabout Mini Golf rounds with friends since I got it.

The mechanism for securing the controller onto the club is identical to previous AMVR controllers; only the location of the mount is different. Slide the controller (with wrist strap attached) into the holster. Click the rubber stopper in so the controller doesn’t move, then loop the wrist strap around the controller as a backup in case you didn’t secure the rubber stopper properly. It’s quite simple.

All major VR golf games allow custom spacing for Quest 3 golf clubs, so it doesn’t take more than 30 seconds to get comfortable with the club in your game of choice.

The only problem I’ve found with this club is its price. Most Quest 3 golf club accessories cost between $30 and $50, depending on the capabilities. This one is normally double that, but AMVR was kind enough to pass along a 25% off coupon for 9to5Google readers, making it more palatable if you’re looking to improve your VR golf scores. Just apply the coupon code 1FD4JYT5 at checkout on Amazon for an extra 25% off the AMVR GA2 golf club.

If you’re serious about your scores in Golf+, Walkabout Mini Golf, or another favorite of yours, this might just be the ultimate enthusiast Quest 3 golf club accessory.

The original definition of "hacking" was making hardware and software do something it wasn't supposed to.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Hacking stories these days mostly involve someone using an army of AI agents to find vulnerabilities in networks and software that were carefully hidden in plain sight. Today, for a change, we have a story about hacking in its original meaning — twisting computing artifacts into purposes not in their design spec. David Oberhollenzer, aka Goliath, a greybeard in spirit if not in shade, crafted a 100% valid ZIP file that's simultaneously an archive, BIOS-bootable, and a Multiboot-compatible OS image.

You can unpack the ZIP file just like any other, boot it using Linux's GRUB, QEMU, or any other Multiboot-compatible loader (even if imaged to different media), or alternatively, perform the finest party trick: image-write it to a floppy and boot from it directly from BIOS on any compatible PC, without modification.

Much like me, that sequence of words may be triggering a head-tilt reminiscent of a confused puppy, so we'll explain. The first thing you need to know is that unlike most file types, the metadata (in this case, file directory) of a ZIP is actually at the end of the archive. Up to that point, the data is comprised of every compressed file in sequence.

The file packs all have a predictable structure: "PK" followed by bytes 03 04, metadata (including name), some extra/comment fields, and then the file's contents. Notably, any file can be stored uncompressed, and Goliath made use of that for the very first file, called ZIPHEAD.COM — remember, this is the start of the ZIP archive.

Goliath said that it was "easy" to make the ZIP file a valid Multiboot system image. A valid image only needs to contain bytes 0x1BADB002 in the first 8 KiB, followed by some flags and a checksum. It was trivial to place that datum in ZIPHEAD's data, along with the location of where the bootloader lies.

Grub or QEMU don't care about anything else in the image, as once they have the initialization information, from that point it's the bootloader's problem. The actual bootloader, predictably, is in ZIPHEAD's uncompressed data, and the image will happily boot directly, or, say, from a floppy.

Making the same exact archive bootable via a standard PC BIOS took a little more work and some clever shenanigans. Making a disk bootable is simple enough: the BIOS reads the first exact 512 bytes of the disk's contents, and if they end with bytes 0x55AA, then it's bootable, and the BIOS starts executing whatever code is the first byte.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Placing 0x55AA precisely at position 510 of the ZIP, already in ZIPHEAD's contents, is once again simple, and won't corrupt the Multiboot image, as if you'll recall, the Multiboot spec is flexible with data locations. But you may wonder: once the BIOS runs code in sequence starting from the ZIP's first byte, then ZIPHEAD's header ("PK" + 0x0304, plus all metadata) surely is garbage for practical purposes, and not proper code? Well, yes, but actually no.

The first four bytes represent CPU instructions that don't write anything to memory, so they're harmless, other than a push-to-stack. The next few belong to ZIPHEAD's metadata, and Goliath massaged those values to represent instructions that would either be innocuous or perform operations he could use, namely using the modification time bytes as instructions to jump further down the data.

Sounds simple, but the actual process of choosing bytes that represent (1) non-crashy CPU instructions, (2) useful code for setting up the boot process, and (3) still represent a valid file header in a ZIP archive is far trickier than the above. Do go and check out the full blog post if you want all the details.

#10244. Top 6 AI Detector Tools in 2026: Features, Accuracy Claims and When to Trust Them

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

• A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

• Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

• Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

• Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

• Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it says it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your plan. It says to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

Strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and says other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The company’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and plan prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

Copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it says it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

Limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid plan prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, says very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

Sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

Strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page says false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

The table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

• Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

• Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

• Moving targets. New models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

• Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

OpenAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

• Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

• Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and update as new models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

• Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical"

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function."""

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0})

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan")

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan")

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}")

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

• Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

• Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

• Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

• Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

They can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

Sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

#10243. How to build scalable web apps with OpenAI's Privacy Filter

All three are built on gradio.Server, which lets you pair custom HTML/JS frontends with Gradio's queueing, ZeroGPU allocation, and gradio_client SDK. In all these apps, gradio.Server plays the same backend role, and that consistency is exactly what makes it really powerful.

Try it at ysharma/OPF-Document-PII-Explorer.

User problem. You want to read a PII-heavy document (a contract, a resume, an exported chat log) with every detected span highlighted by category, a filter in the sidebar, and a summary dashboard up top. The reading experience should feel like a normal document, not a form.

What gr.Server does here. You could wire this up in Blocks with gr.HighlightedText and a sidebar, and it would work. The reading experience we wanted (serif body, category filters that toggle CSS classes client-side instead of re-running the model, a summary dashboard that doesn't force a page re-render) was easier to hand-author than to compose. gr.Server lets us serve the reader view as a single HTML file and expose the model behind one queued endpoint:

Note the decorator: @server.api(name="analyze_document"), not a plain @server.post. That's the piece that plugs the handler into Gradio's queue, so concurrent uploads are serialized, @spaces.GPU composes correctly on ZeroGPU, and the same endpoint is reachable from both the browser and gradio_client with no duplicated code. The browser calls it with the Gradio JS client:

User problem. You want to share an image or any screenshot (a Slack thread, a receipt, a Stripe dashboard) with black bars over the PII. You want to toggle bars on and off, drag them to reposition, or draw one by hand for anything the model missed, then export the result.

What gr.Server does here. gr.ImageEditor supports layered annotation and is a reasonable starting point for image redaction. The workflow we wanted (per-bar category metadata, toggle all bars in a category at once, client-side PNG export at natural resolution with no server round-trip) was cleaner to build on a custom frontend. gr.Server hands back pixel rectangles from one queued endpoint and lets the canvas own everything else:

The frontend invokes it with client.predict("/anonymize_screenshot", { image: handle_file(file) }), the same pattern as above. Toggles, drags, new-bar drawing, and PNG export all happen in the browser; edits never round-trip to the server.

User problem. You want a pastebin that redacts before sharing. You paste a log line, an email, a support ticket. You get two URLs back. The public one serves the redacted version with , , placeholders, following the redaction convention from the official blog examples. The private one is gated by a token you keep and shows the original with spans highlighted.

What gr.Server does here. This app needs two distinct GET routes for the same paste ID, one public and one token-gated, and the URL shape matters because the reveal URL is the thing you keep. gr.Server works here because it's a FastAPI app underneath — which is also why @server.api and plain @server.get can sit side by side in the same process. Note: this can also be built with gr.Blocks() by mounting custom routes with FastAPI :

A daemon thread evicts expired pastes every 30 seconds. The whole service, including storage, is about 200 lines of application code because everything lives in one process.

The split across all three apps is the same — anything that touches the model goes through @server.api, everything else stays on plain FastAPI routes:

@server.api gives you Gradio's queue (serialized requests, correct @spaces.GPU composition on ZeroGPU, progress events) and it's what the browser hits through @gradio/client. The same endpoint is also what gradio_client users hit from Python — one function, two SDKs, no duplicated code. Plain @server.get/@server.post are reserved for the static surfaces: HTML pages, file lookups, cheap dict reads. That's the rule of thumb from the gradio.Server intro post, and it's what makes these three apps feel consistent even though their UIs are very different.

One gap I keep hitting for clinical notes outside EN: taxonomy coverage ≠ “run the same 8 labels on another language/domain.” Locale clinical text needs entity classes and distractors that the EN consumer schema doesn’t encode; otherwise you measure a different product than the one you deploy. Synthetic labeled notes help for that coverage test before anyone claims compliance.

Curious whether you’ve tried feeding clinical-style notes (even synthetic) through the same 8 labels and where the misses concentrate.

#10240. Proton Pass is up to 60% off for Black Friday—and it does way more than just store your passwords

There’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

Proton Pass is designed to take that friction out of your day. It creates strong, unique passwords, remembers them for you, and fills them in when you log in. But it also handles something a password alone can’t: keeping your real email address out of another retailer’s database.

For Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other important parts of your digital life — organized.

Take a look at Proton’s Black Friday offers, starting at $1.99 per month

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

Proton Pass does that work for you. When you sign up for a website, its password generator can create a strong password that’s completely unique. Save it in your vault, and Proton Pass can fill in your credentials when you return.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

Proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

An alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

It’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

Proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

When you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

Proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

Proton’s offers are available to new users and include a 30-day money-back guarantee.

Key presses turn into bursts of reads and writes to play the game.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Doom now runs on a USB flash drive’s built-in LCD and is played by copying files to and from it, as hardware hacker Aaron Christophel showed in a teardown video. The marking on the drive’s display chip had been removed, but an open debug port let him extract its firmware, which enabled identification. He was then able to use AI to reverse-engineer the hardware and get the game running on the drive’s screen.

The off-the-shelf drive, the MOVESPEED MSSU10, has USB-A on one end and USB-C on the other, and the 128GB model, the smallest capacity in the range, cost him about 50 euros. Its screen normally shows status data such as transfer speed, how full the drive is, and its temperature.

The main flash controller is the Silicon Motion SM2320G, one we have reviewed in portable SSDs like the Kingston XS2000 and Lexar SL660 Blaze, with a separate C*Core CCM4101 microcontroller — which has 2MB of flash and a small amount of RAM to itself — for the 428 x 142 color LCD. The NAND carries SanDisk markings. All of this is fairly standard portable SSD hardware, aside from the display.

The drive’s metal body uses heavily glued plastic end pieces but, past that, the display lifts off first and unplugs. The board slides out after the USB-C end cap is removed, in this case with minor cosmetic damage inflicted. The display chip’s marking is scrubbed, most likely with a laser, by the hacker’s reckoning, which can hinder identification and tinkering. Luckily, a probe on the debug pads, ground, and a 3.3V pin connected on the first try, and memory was immediately readable.

The bootloader returned a version string dated 2023, followed by the full firmware, which helped greatly with identification. He says the chip is marketed as one for security — for fingerprint readers and access control, for example — but no related features were found to be enabled for this drive. He also discovered that, although the data sheet and stock firmware declare a 200 MHz operating clock frequency, it measured 40.2 MHz. This is unexplained.

One critical issue is immediately apparent: how do you play on a drive with no buttons? The display chip has no USB connection of its own and, from the connected PC or host, it only sees the storage controller’s activity, which it uses to gauge transfer speed. The primary storage controller has read and write counters, and the chip pulls these every 50 ms over I2C. Christophel says this is far easier than relying on a single physical button, as he did on a previous power bank mod.

The solution, then, is a PC script, doomctl.py, which turns key presses into small, timed transfers in each direction. The commands are simply encoded as transfer rates, at five levels per direction, and each read/write pair can map to a certain button combination. Arrow keys are for movement and turning, Space or Ctrl for firing and opening doors, and M for the menu, keeping it simple. Ordinary copying, without the script, can still steer, but the control scheme is much nicer.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Performance is…well, not really playable at about 13 frames per second, although the game logic runs at Doom’s normal 35 ticks per second. This is why he names the chip’s clock as the biggest potential performance gain. The game itself is built on DMC100-DOOM, Artur Bieniek’s port for very small microcontrollers. Only the first map, E1M1, fits in the chip’s flash, and no sound is produced as the drive lacks a buzzer. Christophel did play the level end to end, noting the low resolution.

AI did the heavy lifting: the reverse engineering as well as the port, and Christophel said, “I would not be able to do such a thing in a few hours.”

The open-source project, with its code and prebuilt firmware published, is likely to draw attention and may spawn similar hacks. The tools required are relatively minimal, mainly a debug probe, and he does suggest backing up the stock firmware before trying. For his own unit, he put it back together to use as a normal drive, but one that can still play Doom, if so desired.
