Minisforum’s smallest and cheapest mini PC packing Intel's Wildcat Lake silicon is here. It is small, quiet, and easy to stow away, but this machine's performance is really only for light workloads.

Capable enough for home office and media consumption

Only old or lightweight games and emulators are playable

Not a cheap option unless you have spare parts and go barebones

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Minisforum’s Intel-based M2 line includes mini PCs with powerful processors such as the Core Ultra X7 Processor 358H (with 16C/16T CPU and B390 graphics), and the Core Ultra 7 356H (16C/16T). But there are more modest systems, too. The M2 Air-304 here is the most affordable option, based around the Intel Core 3 processor 304 with its 5C/5T CPU (1x Cougar Cove P-core and 4x Darkmont LP E-cores) and an iGPU with just a single Xe3 core.

No surprise, the little brother in the pack, both in terms of physical size and computing resources, is the most affordable. It currently starts at $263 for a barebones version. However, our test sample with 16GB DDR5-5600, a 500GB SSD, and Windows 11 Pro is listed at $559 - direct. That’s an introductory price, and Minisforum’s small text threatens that our configuration will bump up to $699 at some point in the future. Such a rise would put this product offering on very shaky ground, and we see B&H Photo has already raised the price at $729.

Overall, this Mini PC was pleasant to use, though. It ran quietly and only strained in gaming and productivity benchmarks which put it under loads that casual users aren’t going to be running on such a machine.

The Mini M2 Air looks stylish enough, and feels solid. Looks can be deceiving, though, and the top shell is a silver colored plastic, not a metallic alloy. Sometimes a metal shell can be used to help conduct away heat, but that seems less important with this actively cooled machine with a 15W processor. We note that there are thermal pads connecting the installed RAM and SSD to the bottom of this mini PC, which is metal.

A VESA mounting bracket is provided in the box if you prefer to hide the tiny device out of sight. It doesn’t have a remote power switch like the MSI Cubi NUC AI+ 3MG we reviewed earlier in the year, though, so you’ll have to consider reachability. A simple LED-lit power button is on the front of the device, alongside a couple of handy ports (more on the ports later). It also has a reset / clear CMOS hole on the front, and a Kensington lock slot on the rear.

Minisforum’s component choices mean this is a particularly small and light mini PC. The official M2 Mini specs state it is 112 x 112 x 37.15mm, which is roughly 4.4 x 4.4 x 1.5-inches. That’s a volume of 0.47 liters. It weighs in at just 440 grams, which is 0.97 pounds.

The power supply isn’t built-in. There’s a surprisingly bulky 65W power brick in the box, which connects to using a detachable figure-eight cable. However, this mini PC can be powered by USB-C, too, so you could pack a far more compact multipurpose power brick if portability is important.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Intel Core 3 304 (5C/5T) ‘Wildcat Lake,’ up to 4.3 GHz, 15W

Intel integrated graphics, 1x Xe3 core runs at up to 2.3 GHz, supports up to 3x displays

16GB in single SODIMM slot which can fit up to a 64GB DDR5-6400 module

1x M.2 2280 PCIe 4.0 x4 NVMe SSD slot (up to 2TB), microSD card expansion

Front: 2x USB-A 3.2 Gen 2, 3.5mm audio. Rear: 1x USB4 (40Gbps, DP Alt Mode, PD), 1x USB-C 10Gbps, 1x USB 2.0, 2x HDMI 2.0, 2x RJ-45 2.5GbE LAN, DC-IN. Side: microSD card slot.

Windows 11; barebone model available without OS

$559.00 limited-time price(16GB RAM, 500GB SSD, Windows 11 Pro)

On the front of the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 there are 2x USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 ports and a 3.5mm audio jack. Turn it to the side and you’ll see the microSD card slot. Then, around the back you have access to 1x USB4 (40Gbps, DP Alt Mode, PD), 1x USB-C 10Gbps, 1x USB 2.0, 2x HDMI 2.0, 2x RJ-45 2.5GbE LAN, and a DC-IN barrel jack.

Some might like to have at least one of the Type-C ports on the front, instead of two Type-As. But for its size the Mini M2 Air packs quite a few ports, including the very capable USB4, two HDMI ports, and two Ethernet ports. Realistically, a machine like this won’t be connected to oodles of wired peripherals, but if you found the port count lacking, USB4 allows for a capable and fast dock.

Wireless connectivity seems adequate, with an M.2 2230 card inside providing Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.4. I had no problems with either during the test period. The wireless card is socketed. It's located under the SSD, making it easy to repair or upgrade down the line.

Accessing the components inside the Minisforum Mini M2 Air is straightforward, but you need to peel off all the four rubber feet to get to four long fastening screws. When they’re removed, just flip off the metal bottom to access the M.2 slots and SODIMM. Be aware there’s some adhesive force holding this metal plate in place, due to the sticky thermal pads on the RAM and storage.

There’s just a single M.2 2280 storage slot and one SODIMM slot, both populated. That means, there’s no way to upgrade the RAM than swapping the module you already have in place. Our sample came with a 16GB DDR5-5600 SODIMM, but the system supports up to DDR5-6400. This only non-barebones configuration also came with a 500GB SSD in the M.2 slot.

We have Intel’s latest 18A silicon inside this tiny PC, but not that much of it. Our review unit came with an Intel Core 3 304 "Wildcat Lake" chip that runs up to 4.3 GHz. Previous mini PCs based on Intel 300 series mobile silicon like the previously MSI and the GMKtec Evo-T2 came with a 16C/16T CPU. However, here we have just 5C/5T, and that’s just one performance core supported by four low power efficiency (LPE) cores.

Still, single core performance continues to be important for system and app responsiveness. The proof of the pudding is in the testing, though. And while this system felt perfectly usable in Windows 11, internet browsers, and word processing — preparing and writing this review, for example — the benchmarks are somewhat tougher.

As we expected, the single core tests show Wildcat Lake has some bite. It easily beats its AMD-based rivals in the POV Ray single core rendering tests, for example. Moreover, in tests like Cinebench 2024 single core, the Mini M2 Air might trail the pack, but not by very much. It's roughly 107 points is actually within touching distance of the 120 points scored by ‘high performance’ mini PCs like the Beelink SER10 MAX (Gorgon Point) and MSI Cubi NUC AI+ 3MG (Panther Lake).

Multicore tests exposed obvious weaknesses of the 5C/5T CPU configuration with single-channel RAM. All the other mini PCs we’ve tested this year come with 12C/24T (AMD) or 16C/16T (Intel), so the productivity benchmarks we run which can take advantage of multithreading for demanding rendering or encoding tasks make the Minisforum here seem weak. However, it might still be acceptable for transcoding a short video or two, occasionally, as long as you aren’t in a rush. If you are coming from an older, less efficient desktop sporting something like an i7-7700K or i5-10400, this 15W Wildcat Lake chip is an improvement in both single and multicore performance.

During our demanding tests, the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 stayed cool and quiet thanks to its 15W processor and capable cooling.

For anything other than the most casual gaming or emulation of older consoles you should look at other devices. We’ve looked at Intel 300 silicon powered devices with iGPUs packing 12 Xe3 cores, and four Xe3 cores, but this just has one, and it is further hampered by sharing the single-channel system RAM.

Prepare to see some low frame rates / scores in our standard tests. I felt that some of these tests probably shouldn’t be run on this mini PC, but did it anyway, for completeness. However, some 3DMark benchmarks simply wouldn’t run, as Intel has pruned the features that work on this iGPU due to limited resources. For example, 3DMark Solar Bay doesn’t run on this system, and neither does Speed Way. Error messages about unsupported hardware pop up when you try these tests.

Steel Nomad ran, though, and the Minisforum and its solo Xe3 core achieved a score of 135. The aforementioned Evo-T2 with Intel Core Ultra X7 358H and (B390) iGPU with 12x Xe3 cores scored 1,624. That’s incredibly close to 12x faster than the Core 3 304’s ‘Intel Graphics.’ A score of 135 means Steel Nomad ran at just a little more than 1 FPS, which actually doesn’t hurt your eyes to watch as much as 10 FPS.

Using the multi-scene benchmarks built into Shadow of the Tomb Raider and Cyberpunk 2077 using our standard settings selections resulted in some unpleasant experiences. Performance of no better than 10 or 12 FPS was observed in these tests. To achieve 25 or even 30 FPS in these titles I found that reducing the game resolution to 720p and low/lowest settings would just about get there.

So, for some actual fun on the Mini M2 Air I decided to try the latest version of the Sony PSP emulator PPSSPP and play some Wipeout Pure. I managed to run this game on my 1440p monitor with a 6x render resolution, and it achieved a nice steady 60 FPS, delivering an enjoyable futuristic racing experience. It would also therefore likely be good for retro emulation of similar era and older consoles as well as home computers.

During my day-to-day use, the Minisforum system consumed around 9W when idling on the desktop. When under the heaviest loads I threw at it, the highest system power consumption I saw was around 31W.

I didn't find it surprising that this low-power system ran cool and quiet. System tools showed that during light activities like browsing the web the CPU temperature remained in the low 30s Celsius. Playing games or benchmarking for length periods, I never saw the reported CPU temperature rise beyond the low 70s Celsius.

Minisforum’s tiny mini PC was a quiet operator at idle and under load. My measurements from about half a foot in front of the device show noise levels under 30 dBA at idle, which is very quiet and actually said to be beneath the measurement threshold of my meter. Stressing the system with simultaneous CPU and GPU loads I managed to observe just a reading of a little over 37 dBA from the system.

The Mini M2 Air ships with Windows 11 Pro installed in the configuration we received. I found no pre-installed bloatware. The official specs don’t mention compatibility with other OSes like Linux.

Minisforum sells this mini PC with a two-year warranty and a 30-day money-back guarantee.

Minisforum sells only two Elite Mini M2 Air-304 configurations in the U.S. There’s a barebones model, or the configuration we tested with pre-installed RAM, SSD, and OS.

At the time of writing our 16GB / 500GB / Windows 11 Pro configuration is listed by the mini PC maker at $559 but the product page says the price is normally $699. The barebone model is currently $263, discounted from $329. We don’t know when the prices might get adjusted. However, we’ve noted U.S. retailers like B&H Photo are now selling the 16GB / 500GB model at $729.

Though the Mini M2 Air’s performance may lack in performance, it also probably the smallest cheapest, and least power-hungry mini PC we’ve tested all year. If these kinds of qualities are important to you, the Minisforum might be appealing.

It is admirable that this mini PC is so small but leaves RAM and storage upgrades on the table for later. Other positives are the sturdy build, despite the use of plastic for the top shell, and a good port selection considering its size. In addition to being easy to hide due to its small stature, and supplied VESA mount, you probably won’t hear it very much, either.

Of course, the performance is a weakness that can’t be ignored, especially in the context of our ever-growing tested mini PCs chart from 2026. It is great to see this latest-gen processor barebones at just over $260 direct from Minisforum. If you have a spare DDR5 SODIMM and SSD, perhaps from a laptop upgrade or wherever, this might help you get a new mini PC system up and running cheaply. However, the 16GB RAM and 500GB SSD (and Windows 11 Pro license) currently more than doubles the list price (it adds $296). That’s a bit painful.

Furthermore, if the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air ever rises to its apparent MSRP of $699, we’d definitely look elsewhere. Around this price, especially during sale periods, you can shop for mini PCs employing far more powerful previous-gen processors. One good alternative candidate might be the Geekom IT13 Max 2026 we reviewed in August at $799. Price trackers show this Core Ultra 185H machine with 24GB RAM has been available for under $600 with discount / coupon over the last few months. There are also a lot of capable older gen AMD mini PCs to ponder over at attractive prices.

#10197. Pixel Tag is a brilliant Band-Aid on a Find Hub network Google can’t easily fix

The Google Pixel Tag is here and, at least so far, it’s really good. But fresh hardware and some new features can’t fix the core problem. Google’s Find Hub network has been restricted from the very start, and it’s not something Google can easily fix.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

The good news on Pixel Tag: this is a well-built tracker that, unlike others, is the clear product of the hardware having direct access to the software. Little touches like being able to adjust ringer volume on the fly combine nicely with UWB – the latter something we rarely see on third-party devices largely due to Apple – all things that elevate the Find Hub tracker to what we called the new “gold standard.”

The bad news: this is still a Find Hub tracker.

Google’s Find Hub network has improved dramatically over the two years since its launch. Where Google originally had to admit that tracking performance was lacking (a nice way of putting it, frankly), improvements started arriving in 2025. We noticed that the network seemed to be working much better a few months after its wide rollout, and Google later confirmed speed improvements.

But, ultimately, the Find Hub network is still reeling from how it debuted.

Again, it’s gotten better since then, but it’s still not as good as it should be. Samsung’s network, limited solely to Galaxy phones, shouldn’t outperform Google’s. Find Hub trackers should be just as good as AirTags and the third-party trackers that work with Apple’s network. They’re just not, and I truly do believe it all boils down to this initial choice. One of the reasons this is getting better is that Google has been pushing users to the “all areas” setting during the setup of a new device – I’ve noticed this on some recent devices I set up, but it’s not been completely consistent just yet. That’s a good step forward but, even if it is the new default, that still requires millions of users to upgrade their devices, and we’ve never been in a better time to not upgrade your phone.

All of that is to say, the Pixel Tag isn’t fixing this problem. Surely, it’ll give Google some needed fire to fix the problem, but new hardware isn’t the solution. That’s something I was discussing with 9to5Google readers on our review. UWB is a tentpole feature of the Pixel Tag, but it doesn’t change the network problems, it just improves precision finding. We needed a first-party tracker like this regardless of the state of the network, something that really takes advantage of the platform and pushes it forward, but it’s just a quick fix, a Band-Aid.

What do you think? Have you found the Find Hub network reliable enough, or is there still room for improvement? Sound off in the comments below!

#10196. OlmoEarth v1.1: A more efficient family of Earth observation models

🧠 Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/olmoearth | 📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth_v1_1 | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/olmoearth_pretrain

We released OlmoEarth (v1) in November 2025. Since then, partners have applied it across a wide range of tasks, from tracking mangrove change to classifying drivers of forest loss to producing country-scale crop-type maps in days, scaling deployments to national, continental, and global areas. Every release moves us closer to our mission: bringing state-of-the-art AI to organizations and communities working to protect people and our planet.

When OlmoEarth processes satellite imagery to make predictions across tens to hundreds of thousands of square kilometers, efficiency shapes what’s possible. Over the full lifecycle of running OlmoEarth – data export, preprocessing, inference, and post-processing – compute is by far the highest cost. A more efficient model means we can support more partners on the OlmoEarth Platform, and that anyone running OlmoEarth on their own can leverage this technology faster and at lower expense.

That’s why we built OlmoEarth v1.1: a new family of models that cuts compute costs by up to 3x while maintaining OlmoEarth v1's performance on a mix of research benchmarks and tasks we’ve constructed with partners.

The OlmoEarth models are transformer-based models, one of the dominant architectures in machine learning today. To process remote sensing data, we first convert it into a sequence of tokens the model can ingest.

Two important levers control efficiency in transformer-based models: model size (this is why we release a family of models, so users can pick the size that fits their compute budget) and token sequence length. Compute costs scale quadratically with the token sequence length, so even small reductions can meaningfully cut the cost of running the model.

MACs, or multiply-accumulate operations, estimate the computation needed for one model forward pass; lower MACs generally mean cheaper, faster inference. The y-axis is inverted because lower average rank is better. Labels show model family and size. All plotted points use the pasted MAC/rank values.

This raises an important question for transformer-based remote sensing models: what should a token represent?

Take Sentinel-2 imagery, a common modality we process. A Sentinel-2 input will be some tensor with a height and width (H, W representing the latitudinal and longitudinal pixels), a temporal dimension T, and 12 Sentinel-2 channels ([H, W, T, D=12]).

Currently, we split the data into resolution-based patches. Concretely, this means that we will pick some spatial patch size p, and split our overall Sentinel-2 image into patches of size p x p:

For each patch, we create a token per timestep per resolution. So a Sentinel-2 input with 2 timesteps yields 6 tokens per patch (2 timesteps x 3 resolutions, 10m, 20m, and 60m).

In total, a[H, W, T, D=12] Sentinel-2 input will yield H/p x W/p x T x 3 tokens.

Using a unique token per resolution is a common technique when processing Sentinel-2 data—Galileo and SatMAE both take this approach, and SatMAE shows significantly better results when doing it. However, it is not universal: CROMA is a model that only uses a single token for all bands, regardless of resolution. Because token counts compound multiplicatively, collapsing resolutions into a single token produces three times fewer tokens and material savings across pretraining, fine-tuning, and inference.

Naively combining the tokens in this way leads to significant performance drops, including a 10 ppt drop on m-eurosat kNN (a common benchmark task for remote sensing models). We hypothesize that separating Sentinel-2 bands into different tokens makes it easier for OlmoEarth to model important cross-band relationships.

Merging tokens without impacting performance required us to modify our pre-training regimen. We describe those changes in detail in our paper.

The result is a model family that does more with less. At every size, OlmoEarth v1.1 runs up to three times cheaper than OlmoEarth v1, making frequent, planet-scale map refreshes more affordable for every team running OlmoEarth. If you're using a model from the original OlmoEarth family, try OlmoEarth v1.1. It provides similar performance to OlmoEarth v1 while requiring one third of the compute, though we have seen some regressions (see our technical report for more details). If it works for your task, you should see a significant speedup during fine-tuning and inference.

Pretrained remote sensing models have many degrees of freedom, which makes them hard to study. When performance shifts, is it the architecture, the dataset, or the pre-training algorithm?

We train OlmoEarth v1.1 on the same dataset as OlmoEarth v1, so any differences between the two isolate the effect of methodological changes. We hope this advances understanding of scientific principles when pretraining models for remote sensing.

Check out the OlmoEarth v1.1 weights and training code, including the weights for our Base, Tiny, and Nano models.

#10194. Harness, Scaffold, and the AI Agent Terms Worth Getting Right

When a field evolves quickly, its vocabulary often evolves faster than its shared understanding. Terms start to blur, get reused in different contexts, or become shorthand for ideas that are never fully explained. We are currently seeing this happen in the field of AI Agents, where concepts are getting mixed together, some are renamed, and others are widely used for a few months before quietly disappearing.

This can be overwhelming for newcomers, and even for practitioners trying to keep up with the latest developments. After ICLR 2026, one of us (@ariG23498) posted a question that captured this confusion well:

"What do you mean by the terms 'harness' and 'scaffold' in the context of agents? I have heard a lot of explanations while I was at ICLR, but I could not understand why they did not converge to a single explanation."

This glossary is our attempt to ground the terms that keep coming up without clear, consistent explanations. It is not meant to be a comprehensive dictionary of every term in the field. Instead, we focus on the concepts that are often mixed up, reused in different ways, or assumed to be obvious when they are not.

Most of these terms come up whether you're building an agent, deploying one, or just using tools like Claude Code, Codex, or Hermes Agent. The last section covers concepts specific to training models, which is more relevant if you work on that side of things.

Many of these terms don't have universally accepted definitions yet, and different frameworks use the same word differently. The goal here is not to enforce one correct vocabulary, but to provide a practical mental model that makes discussions easier to follow.

The model is the LLM: it takes text in and produces text out (e.g., Claude, Qwen, GPT, Kimi, DeepSeek…). On its own, it has no memory between calls, and no loop. The model can express the intent to call a tool, but it needs a harness to actually execute it. It answers one prompt and stops. Wrap it in scaffolding and a harness and it becomes an agent.

The behavior-defining layer around the model: system prompt, tool descriptions, how the model's responses get parsed, what it remembers across steps (context management). It shapes how the model sees the world and acts in it, whether during training or at inference.

Products like Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity CLI call the whole thing a harness. Claude Code's own docs say it directly: "Claude Code serves as the agentic harness around Claude." That's the broad use: harness means everything that isn't the model. The scaffold/harness distinction matters most when you need to reason about them separately, as in a training pipeline. You'll also hear "scaffold" used more broadly to cover any infrastructure the harness relies on: hooks, runtime configuration, even directory structure.

Some products like Claude Code and Codex are tightly coupled to their provider's models. Others like Antigravity CLI and Hermes Agent let you plug in any model.

The execution layer inside the agent: it calls the model, handles its tool calls, decides when to stop. The harness is what makes the agent run. Scaffolding, defined above, is what the model works from: its instructions, its tools, its format.

Harness engineering is the discipline of designing this layer well: deciding when the agent should stop, how errors get handled, and what guardrails keep it on track. It applies at both training and inference. Addy Osmani's piece and OpenAI's account of building with Codex both cover this from the inference side.

At evaluation time, the same pattern shows up as an eval harness: instead of collecting training data, it runs a fixed set of scenarios at a model checkpoint and records metrics rather than updating weights.

Some frameworks use orchestrator for a higher-level controller that coordinates work across multiple agents. Unlike a harness, which drives a model through its execution loop, an orchestrator manages agents as units, each running their own harness (see Sub-agents below).

The term comes from reinforcement learning, where an agent is simply a function that takes an observation and returns an action. The environment takes that action and returns a new observation, and the loop repeats. That loop is still at the core of how LLM agents work.

In the LLM world, the term has expanded. An agent is a model plus everything around it that lets it act, not just respond. It turns raw text generation into something that can act in a loop: taking in information, deciding what to do, and acting on the results.

Take a coding agent as a concrete example. The system prompt, tool descriptions, and the output format the model follows form the scaffolding. The loop that calls the model, handles its tool calls, and decides when to stop is the harness. At training time, the harness also runs many of these loops in parallel and feeds the results back to update the model.

In the community, it's usually put as Agent = Model + Harness (@Vtrivedy10 and Will Brown's tweet for reference). If you're not the model, you're the harness. The subtle distinction between harness and scaffold that creates most of the confusion is what the two sections above address.

When people talk about products like Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, they're referring to a specific harness built on top of a specific model, designed and optimized together. Two products using the same underlying model can feel completely different because their harnesses make different choices. And swapping a better model into the same harness also changes the experience. The model, the harness, and the product are three different things.

Designing what goes into the agent's context window: what the model sees at each step, system prompt, tool descriptions, conversation history, retrieved knowledge. It's not a one-time decision: as the model runs, previous turns shape what goes into future calls, and the harness actively manages this throughout the run. It applies at both training and inference, but the cost of getting it wrong is very different. At training, what the model sees shapes what gets learned. Get it wrong and you're retraining. At inference, it's just text: change a prompt and redeploy. The HF Context Engineering Course covers this in depth.

Memory is part of this picture. Short-term memory is what stays in the context window during a single run: conversation history, tool results, previous reasoning. Long-term memory persists across sessions, stored externally and retrieved on demand, then injected back into context when relevant.

A policy is the behavior an agent follows: given any situation, it defines the probability of taking each possible action. In LLM systems, part of that policy is learned in the model weights, but the behavior also depends on the surrounding scaffolding and harness. The same model can behave very differently depending on its prompts, tools, memory, and execution loop.

A policy is not an agent. The policy defines behavior; the agent is the full system that acts in an environment. Wrap a checkpoint in scaffolding and a harness and deploy it, and you get an agent whose behavior is the policy.

How agents reach outside themselves: APIs, code interpreters, databases, web search, file systems. The model expresses the intent to use a tool in a structured format. Modern inference APIs surface this as a first-class object: the harness receives the call directly and routes it to the right function. The result gets fed back into context and the loop continues.

Reusable, structured packages of knowledge that enable multi-step tasks. Where a tool is an action ("run this command"), a skill bundles everything needed to accomplish a goal ("investigate this bug, form a hypothesis, write a fix"). They are portable across agents and loaded on demand. The line between tool, skill, and sub-agent shifts across frameworks. The HF Context Engineering Course covers skills in depth.

An agent called by another agent to handle a specific subtask. It has its own model and scaffold, reasons independently, and returns a result. The calling agent doesn't need to know how it works internally. This is what separates a sub-agent from a tool (a function call) or a skill (packaged knowledge): a sub-agent can itself reason, use tools, and call further sub-agents. The calling agent is sometimes called an orchestrator.

The terms above apply whether you're training or deploying. These four are specific to training, where the agent runs through tasks, gets scored, and its model's weights get updated. Every RL training system for LLMs is built around the same pipeline:

The environment is anything you can interact with: a stateful object that takes an action as input, updates its internal state, and returns an observation. In the LLM context, actions are typically tool calls. A filesystem is a simple example: the action touch foo.txt updates the state by creating the file, and the observation might be the updated file listing. Definitions vary across frameworks.

We recently published a dedicated guide on this, so rather than compress it here, see The Ultimate Guide to RL Environments for a complete breakdown of types, frameworks, and examples.

The trainer is what makes the agent better: it runs many agent episodes, scores the results and uses them to update the inner model's weights. TRL's GRPOTrainer is a concrete example: a single class that handles episode generation, reward scoring, and weight updates.

A rollout is one full agent run from start to finish: what the agent saw, what it did, and what reward it got at each step. It's also called a trajectory or a trace, depending on the context. This is the raw data RL algorithms learn from.

The score that tells the training algorithm whether the model is getting better. It can be verifiable (tests pass/fail, answer matches), or learned (human preferences, LLM-as-judge), sparse (one score at the end of an episode), or dense (a score at each step). This is what the trainer uses to actually update the inner model's weights. For a thorough breakdown of each type, see the Reward Architecture section in Adithya's guide.

Rubrics break the reward into explicit dimensions with weights, rather than a single number. OpenEnv and Verifiers implement rubrics as objects you can combine (WeightedSum, Sequential, Gate).

If any definition feels imprecise or you've encountered a term we've missed, we'd love to hear from you.

Thanks to Pedro Cuenca, Quentin Gallouédec, Shaun Smith, and Adithya S Kolavi for reviewing this post.

The definition of Agent in popular use changes every year :)

We really leaned into Autonomy in this post from last year, but this year it seems to be all about model + harnesses: https://huggingface.co/blog/ethics-soc-7

All in all, the more precise and technically specific the term, the better!

Coding Agent, or Agent CLI – a command-line application, used to launch and manage agent instances (e.g. Opencode, Claude Code, Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, etc)

Agent Definition – a file (Markdown/JSON) that describes how an agent behaves; serves as a blueprint from which instances are created (like a class in Java)

Agent Instance – a running process created from an Agent Definition (like an object instantiated from a class in Java).

Agent / AI Agent – avoid; use the specific term (CLI, Definition, or Instance) depending on what you mean; not to forget that “Agent” can also mean the CI pipeline agent or a human agent

it's a standardization protocol that makes the Tool Use → Harness connection much cleaner and more interoperable. The glossary describes what agents do; MCP is a specification for how they do the tool-calling part reliably across different vendors and implementations.

Appreciate the nice writeup. Can we add a) Leaderboard, b) Benchmark

Really useful glossary, and I especially appreciate the attempt to separate the model, harness, scaffold, tools, context, and training loop.

One concern I have is with standardizing on “scaffolding” as the term for the behavior-defining layer around the model. To me, “scaffolding” already feels quite overloaded, specifically in software projects. It is used extensively in code generation, and more narrowly by framework generators to create routes, controllers, models, migrations, components, tests, and other boilerplate structures.

I wonder whether “rigging” might be a better candidate. It still relates naturally to the metaphor of a harness, but is less already-standardized in adjacent software and AI contexts. In the horse/cart sense, rigging is the arrangement that attaches the harness to the thing being pulled and makes the whole setup usable. That feels close to what this layer does for an agent: system prompt, tool descriptions, response formats, memory/context rules, and other configurations that connect the model to the operational environment in a particular way.

#10193. Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services

LiteRT in Google Play services is Android's on-device inference runtime for custom models, handling more than a trillion inferences a day across billions of devices. Today, it gets its biggest upgrade yet: GPU inference that runs about 1.4x faster than the legacy GPU delegate, powered by ML Drift and available through the new CompiledModel API, LiteRT’s modern successor to the legacy Interpreter API.

Until now, taking advantage of this faster GPU stack required bundling LiteRT in your app. In our testing, apps that switched to LiteRT in Google Play services are about 8 MB smaller, making them faster to download and lighter on users' devices, because the runtime, including the GPU accelerator, ships once with Play services rather than inside every app. More than 100K Android apps bundle their own copy of LiteRT or TensorFlow Lite today, so the savings add up quickly as apps switch.

If your Android app runs custom ML models on CPU or GPU, we encourage you to switch to LiteRT in Google Play services. You can see it in action in the Google AI Edge Gallery app, where the Scrapbook feature's image segmentation runs on LiteRT in Google Play services.

Developers that adopt LiteRT in Google Play Services enjoy immediate benefits:

LiteRT is the evolution of TensorFlow Lite. It keeps the same .tflite model format you rely on and adds the CompiledModel API, which makes acceleration across fragmented hardware reliable:

Whether you're starting fresh or switching from bundled LiteRT, using LiteRT in Google Play services takes a few lines of code:

If you're already using the legacy Interpreter API in Google Play services, your Interpreter code keeps working on CPU when you switch to play-services-litert. To run on the GPU, move to the CompiledModel API.

Let your coding agent do the work. In Agent Mode, the new LiteRT skill for Android Studio automates the move to LiteRT in Google Play services and the CompiledModel API. Ask it to “migrate my TFLite code to CompiledModel,” or type @litert-runtime, and it switches your app to play-services-litert, rewrites your Interpreter calls, and sets up GPU acceleration with CPU fallback. It can also scaffold a new LiteRT app. Treat it as a strong first pass: review the diff, build, and compare outputs on a real device. Get the skill on GitHub.

Upgrading from legacy APIs? The legacy GPU delegate and custom delegate APIs are deprecated in favor of CompiledModel GPU acceleration and the Compiler Plugin and Dispatch APIs, and NNAPI will be removed starting in 2027. Older SDKs now receive critical security fixes only. Apps you've already shipped keep working, but plan your move to the CompiledModel API now: code that uses deprecated APIs won't compile against the latest SDK, and staying on an older SDK can cause conflicts as your other dependencies move forward. See the release notes for details.

Looking ahead, LiteRT in Google Play services is our foundation for running your own task-specific models on Android, with CPU and GPU acceleration.

Ahead of the holiday season, Google Maps is launching a handy travel itineraries feature alongside a slew of other new capabilities for Ask Maps.

These updates are rolling out starting today on Google Maps for Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and list search are available in all 200+ Ask Maps countries. Know Before You Go in directions and appointment booking are coming first to the US.

#10191. Your SSL certificates can now last 200 days at most: The real risk isn’t renewal

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan. Following the latest update from the CA/Browser Forum, the maximum lifetime of a certificate has fallen from 398 days to 200, and it will drop to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Renewal is no longer an annual chore. It’s an ongoing task that only stays manageable with automation.

So what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes? For many setups, very little will change. For others, one missed renewal can mean an outage. This article explains what’s changing and what to do if you’re in the second group.

Today, an SSL certificate is valid for 200 days at most. The limit applies when a certificate is issued, so the ones you already hold keep their original expiration date.

Where you feel it depends on how your certificates renew. Sites on managed hosting platforms or behind a content delivery network (CDN) usually renew automatically already, often every 90 days, so the new limit changes little. The pressure lands on setups where someone buys a certificate once a year and installs it by hand. At 47 days, that becomes about 12 renewals a year.

A certificate is a promise from a certificate authority that a key really belongs to a domain, and that promise gets less reliable the longer it runs. If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, it stays usable until it expires. Cutting the lifetime shrinks that window, so a problem that once lingered for over a year is now fixed in weeks.

Shorter lifetimes also make revocation, the process for canceling a bad certificate, far less critical. Revocation has never worked perfectly, but a certificate that expires within weeks matters much less if a cancellation doesn’t reach every browser.

Another reason is about people. A task done once a year is easy to forget and hard to check from outside. Browser makers have pushed for years to move the industry onto automatic renewal, on the logic that a process that runs every few weeks gets tested constantly. If it breaks, you notice quickly instead of discovering it on the day the certificate expires.

For most people, the first effect is simply more work. A certificate that once needed attention every year will soon need it every few weeks. Plus, each renewal is a small chance for something to go wrong. Multiply that by dozens of sites, mail servers, and devices, and the chance of one slipping through grows quickly.

The safety nets are also thinner. If you relied on the renewal emails, nothing is watching your certificates now. Additionally, with a shorter life, there’s less time between this should have renewed and this has expired.

An expired certificate doesn’t make a site slow or dated. It makes it unreachable for most visitors. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all show a full-page warning that the connection isn’t private, and most people leave instead of clicking through. If the site uses HSTS, a setting that tells browsers to connect only over secure links, there is often no way to click through at all, and visitors are blocked outright until the certificate is fixed.

The damage doesn’t stop at the home page. Checkouts, contact forms, and logins that depend on the secure connection fail along with it, often without an error message that points at the real cause. Other systems break, too, because apps and integrations that call your site over a secure link refuse to connect to an expired certificate.

Nothing about your site has to change for any of this to happen. A date passes, and a site that worked on Friday is down on Monday. In a 47-day lifetime, that date comes around about every six weeks.

Automatic renewal tools do the heavy lifting well. The failures happen around them:

Look at the five failures above and you’ll see what they share. Each one happens quietly. The renewal job ran, or looked like it did, and nobody checked what the server was actually serving afterwards. Automation can tell you it tried. It can’t tell you the result reached your visitors.

What closes that gap is a check that never relies on your server’s own account of events. Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring does exactly that. It reads the certificate installed on your web server from the cloud, the way a visitor’s browser would, and alerts you before it expires, using thresholds you choose. If a renewal fails quietly, you hear about it from the monitor and not from a customer.

For each certificate, it records the issuing authority, the owner, the issue date, the expiration date, and the days remaining, including on servers that host several certificates behind one address. That last number matters more as lifespans shrink. When a certificate lasts 47 days, the days left is the figure that tells you a renewal is overdue, and you can set your warning against it using the quarter-of-the-lifetime rule covered next.

Once a monitor is watching your certificates, the next question is when it should speak up.

Most expiration alerts are set to a fixed number of days: warn at 30 days left and escalate at seven. That works for a certificate that lasts a year and renews with a month to spare. It breaks when the whole certificate lasts for a limited number of days.

Here’s why: a healthy certificate renews with about a third of its life still left. If your alert appears earlier than that, it goes off on certificates that are doing nothing wrong, and soon everyone ignores it. As lifespans shrink, a fixed 30-day alert will start doing exactly that.

The fix is to set the alerts based on lateness, not on how close the expiry date is. Warn when a quarter of the lifetime is left, since a renewal is overdue by then, and escalate when a tenth is left. Because these are shares of the lifetime, they keep working, however short lifespans get.

The next cut lands on March 15, 2027, so a few checks now will save you from scrambling later:

Shorter lifespans won’t break your site, but a missed renewal will, so fix the quiet failures now while a mistake still costs an afternoon to fix, not a Monday morning outage affecting lots of customers.

If you’d like a second pair of eyes on your certificates, you can start a 30-day free trial of Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring.

#10188. Shipping a Trillion Parameters With a Hub Bucket: Delta Weight Sync in TRL

TL;DR, because you have models to train and we respect that:

Async RL just got a lot cheaper. Read on.

If you read our previous post on the landscape of async RL training, you already know the punchline. Every async RL library, regardless of how it spells "actor model" or which color its NCCL backend is painted, eventually trips over the same root: weight synchronization.

The inference engine speaks the policy of step N. The trainer just finished step N+1. The fresh weights have to get from one side to the other before the inference engine starts drifting hopelessly off-policy. This sits on the critical path whether you are running sync or async: a blocking transfer is wasted idle compute of GPUs not generating tokens. With a sparse delta path you collapse that idle time into seconds, and the trainer does not even have to wait for the inference engine to be ready: it just publishes "weights ready" and uploads the weights to the shared bucket the moment its optimizer step finishes, while the inference engine fetches on its own time.

Fireworks put a very memorable number on this in their post Frontier RL Is Cheaper Than You Think: for a frontier 1T-parameter checkpoint at fp8 (their setting), a full snapshot is 1024 GiB, and that is what conventional wisdom says you have to ship every time you update your rollout fleet. That is the kind of number that gets people to start drawing diagrams with mega-clusters, RDMA fabrics, and dedicated cross-region links. Their measured average delta between adjacent checkpoints lands at 20.3 GiB, or 1.98% of the full model, and "more than 98% of weights in bf16 format remain bit-equivalent between consecutive checkpoints".

Cursor's Composer 2 report tells a parallel story. They run training and inference in different regions and stitch them together with a shared S3 bucket (their exact words), into which the trainer uploads compressed weight diffs every training step. Each cluster independently downloads and reconstructs from the shared delta chain, "requiring no direct connectivity to the training cluster". The two sides never speak to each other about parameters directly. The bucket is the wire.

Both papers agree on three things, and we want to repeat them slowly, because the rest of this post is essentially a faithful open source translation:

The only thing missing was a version of this story that you can pip install. So we wrote one.

Before we wire anything up, it is worth understanding why this whole game is even winnable. The "98% of weights do not change" claim sounds suspiciously like one of those numbers that works in the demo and falls apart in the wild. It is not. It falls out of how bf16 arithmetic works at the learning rates RL uses.

A bf16 number has 7 mantissa bits. Between two consecutive powers of two, there are exactly 27=1282^7 = 12827=128 representable values, so the spacing between adjacent bf16 numbers around ∣w∣|w|∣w∣ is roughly ∣w∣⋅2−7|w| \cdot 2^{-7}∣w∣⋅2−7. An update gets absorbed by the bf16 cast whenever it sits below half of that spacing, i.e., when ∣Δw∣<∣w∣/256|\Delta w| < |w|/256∣Δw∣<∣w∣/256. This is the "bf16 visibility threshold" PULSE plots in their Figure 3.

Now look at what Adam does. At an RL learning rate of, say, 3×10−63 \times 10^{-6}3×10−6, the update to a single weight is: Δw=−η⋅m^v^+ϵ\Delta w = -\eta \cdot \frac{\hat{m}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}} + \epsilon}Δw=−η⋅v^​+ϵm^​

The normalized step m^/(v^+ϵ)\hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon)m^/(v^​+ϵ) is roughly order one, so ∣Δw∣≈η≈3×10−6|\Delta w| \approx \eta \approx 3 \times 10^{-6}∣Δw∣≈η≈3×10−6. For most weights, ∣w∣|w|∣w∣ sits somewhere around 10−210^{-2}10−2 to 10−110^{-1}10−1 (PULSE reports a median of 0.019 for representative LLM weights). The threshold ∣w∣/256|w|/256∣w∣/256 at that magnitude is around 4×10−54 \times 10^{-5}4×10−5 to 4×10−44 \times 10^{-4}4×10−4, which is bigger than the update.

In other words: the optimizer is whispering, and bf16 cannot hear it. The update gets absorbed by rounding, the byte representation of www does not change, and from the inference engine's perspective, this weight did not move. Multiply that by a few hundred million parameters, and you get the >99% sparsity number, for free, with zero approximation.

This is exactly the argument made formal in the PULSE paper (Mihai & Belilovsky, 2026). They define two thresholds. The absorption bound 10η10\eta10η is the conservative worst case for an Adam update, and the effective bound η\etaη is the regime you actually live in. The bf16 visibility threshold is ∣w∣/256|w|/256∣w∣/256. Whenever the update sits below the visibility threshold, it gets absorbed, and the bf16 byte does not change. Their Figure 3 plots both bounds against a cloud of representative LLM weights, and the conclusion is unambiguous: at η=3×10−6\eta = 3 \times 10^{-6}η=3×10−6, the absorption bound itself already sits below the visibility threshold for almost every weight in the model. They measure this empirically across Qwen2.5 (0.5B/1.5B/7B), Llama-3.2-3B, and Gemma-3-4B, and consistently find a mean per-step sparsity of ~99%, with a standard deviation of 0.2 to 0.4% over 400 training steps. The worst-case step stays above 98%. So <1% changed is not a lucky measurement; it is what the arithmetic guarantees.

We do not have to predict this analytically (and indeed, we tried predicting the change mask from Adam's mmm and vvv statistics, but recall was a sad 30%, more on that later). We just need to observe which bytes flipped. That is a tiny boolean tensor per parameter, computed right around the optimizer step.

Here is where the second piece of the story comes in, and where this post stops being a translation of Fireworks/Cursor and starts being a Hugging Face thing.

A Bucket is a repo type on the Hub designed for high-frequency object storage. No commit ceremony, no PR workflow, no LFS quirks. You add files, you list files, you download files. The Python interface is two functions:

That is it. Two function calls and your weights are in flight.

Under the hood, buckets are backed by Xet, the Hub's content-defined chunking storage layer. Xet looks at every file you upload, slices it into chunks based on its actual content (not fixed offsets), and deduplicates against everything already in the bucket. The practical upshot, which is delightful in this context, is that even if we were too lazy to write the sparse encoding and just uploaded full anchors every step, Xet would still only transfer the changed chunks. Sparse encoding + Xet stack: we pay for what moved, and we pay for it once.

This is the open source equivalent of the "shared S3 bucket" both Fireworks and Cursor reach for, except the storage layer already knows about content hashing, your existing HF token already has permission, and it composes natively with the rest of the stack (Spaces, datasets, models).

The full architecture has exactly three boxes and one shared substrate:

The property to internalize, the one Cursor's paper sells hard and that holds verbatim here: the trainer and the rollout server never talk to each other about weights. They exchange a tiny POST containing {"repo_id": ..., "filename": ...}, and that is the entire control plane. The actual byte transfer happens between each side and the bucket, in parallel, with no shared network fabric.

The trainer writes. Replicas read. The Hub does the plumbing.

Now we can open the hood. The protocol has four parts: a wire format, a bucket layout, a 30 line vLLM extension, and a trainer side change detector. It is honestly less code than it sounds.

We picked safetensors for the on-disk and on-wire format. It is already the canonical checkpoint format on the Hub, every reasonable framework can read it, and the header carries arbitrary string metadata. That metadata field is where we hide the protocol.

There are two kinds of files in the bucket.

Anchors look like a normal checkpoint: one tensor per parameter, full bf16 weights, written every NNN syncs (we default to N=10N=10N=10).

Deltas are the interesting bit. For each parameter that actually changed, we store two entries: a flat int32 tensor of element indices, and a bf16 tensor of values at those indices.

The cadence is straightforward: anchor every Nth step, delta in between. Both end up in the same bucket under anchors/ and deltas/ prefixes. Each new inference replica only needs to grab the most recent anchor and then replay the deltas since.

The trainer needs to know which bf16 elements actually flipped. We do this with a tiny BF16ChangeDetector that registers a pre-step and post-step hook on the optimizer:

The actual code in the PR has a bit more plumbing (matching optimizer param objects to model params via data_ptr(), because Accelerate wraps them as different Python objects), but the idea fits on a napkin: snapshot, step, diff.

This is ground truth. We tried the more elegant path of predicting the mask from Adam's mmm and vvv statistics, using the bf16 ULP threshold directly. It works in principle. In practice, recall was around 30%, which means we would have shipped a delta missing two thirds of the actual updates. Adam's normalization is messy enough that the analytical threshold is not tight. So we just compare bytes. It costs one bf16 CPU snapshot of the model on the trainer side, which we are willing to pay.

The four phases of the new _sync_weight flow are:

The line that matters is the parenthesis. Inference was paused for 1.1 seconds. The remaining 9.4 seconds were spent uploading, which occurred while the rollout server was still generating tokens. With NCCL, we were paying the full sync time as pause time. Here we are paying for it as background time.

vLLM has a clean abstraction for this called WeightTransferEngine. We implement a DeltaWeightTransferEngine whose receive_weights method is, in spirit:

We register it via vLLM's --worker-extension-cls flag, which means no fork of vLLM is required. You install TRL into the same image as vLLM, point the CLI at our class, and you are done.

Worth mentioning: vLLM itself has an in-flight effort to land sparse weight transfer natively, vllm-project/vllm#40096. It adds receive_sparse_weights() and trainer_send_sparse_weights() directly on the WeightTransferEngine base class, with patches encoded as (indices, values) and applied in place via index_copy_(), removing the GPU/CPU validation roundtrip entirely. The PR reports a transfer of 0.16 MB in 0.40 ms for a sparse patch on Qwen3-1.7B versus 942 MB in 192 ms for a full dense send.

One honest caveat in our implementation on the inference side: we keep a CPU bf16 snapshot of the model so we can reconstruct full tensors from sparse (indices, values) patches, because load_weights in vLLM today expects full tensors. Once #40096 (or its successor) lands and exposes an in-place sparse load_weights path, we can apply the indices directly on the GPU and drop the snapshot!

This is the part we are smug about. Everything we have described so far works on your laptop, but the point of routing weights through a Hub bucket is that the trainer and the rollout server do not have to live anywhere near each other. So we ran a fully disaggregated training with three machines, none of which share a network:

Setting this up is genuinely a few hf CLI calls. The vLLM Space's Dockerfile is essentially the upstream vLLM image plus pip install trl@... plus the entrypoint:

And kick off training from anywhere on the planet that can talk HTTPS:

The trainer never opens a port. The Space never sees the trainer's IP. The Wordle environment does not know either of them exists. They all talk to the Hub. Training converged on the immediate-EOS sanity check, then on real Wordle rollouts: reward went up, delta payloads stayed in the 20 to 35 MB band, and the inference-paused window per sync stayed around a second. The full run logs are linked in the companion PR.

Async RL training without a cluster. If you have one GPU and a Hugging Face account, you can now do real disaggregated training. Your trainer is on the GPU; your rollout fleet lives in Spaces; your environment lives in another Space; weights move through a bucket. This used to require either a colocated setup (with all the throughput compromises that brings) or a real cluster with shared networking. It does not anymore.

Multi-replica inference, for free. Stand up two vLLM Spaces, or ten. They all pull from the same bucket. Xet content-addresses storage so consecutive anchors share chunks at rest (which keeps your bucket from blowing up), and the Hub's edge cache makes repeated downloads of the same file cheap to serve. Want a globally distributed rollout fleet? That is now a small DevOps exercise, not a research project.

A wire format you can debug with your existing tools. A delta is a safetensors file. You can safe_open it from a notebook, list its keys, inspect the indices, compute the sparsity yourself. We have spent enough hours in tcpdump on opaque NCCL streams to appreciate this.

A path to frontier scale. The 20 to 35 MB number is for Qwen3-0.6B. The interesting question is what the curve looks like once you turn the dial up. Let us do the napkin math.

Take Llama-3.1-405B. In bf16 that is 810 GB on disk. PULSE measures ~99% mean per-step sparsity at RL learning rates, so the actual delta sits around 1% of the parameters. Their deployment-measured encoding hits 108 MB on a 7B model, which is the ~130× reduction PULSE reports. Scaled linearly to 405B, the delta lands at roughly 6 GB per step.

What does that buy you in wall-clock? NCCL is fast inside a cluster, sure. Assume a generous 100 GB/s aggregate broadcast bandwidth (multi-node, RDMA, the works). A full sync is 810 GB / 100 GB/s ≈ 8 seconds of inference pause, every step. With the delta path, the trainer streams 6 GB to a bucket in the background while generation keeps running, and the rollout server's actual paused window is just the apply step, which on this scale lands at a couple of seconds. So even before we leave the cluster, delta cuts the visible pause by 4× and the bytes on the wire by ~130×.

Now leave the cluster. NCCL straight up does not work across clouds. Once you want a rollout fleet in us-east, another in eu-west, maybe one in a Hugging Face Space, the bucket-based path is the only path. At 1 GB/s of usable internet bandwidth, a single full broadcast would take 13 minutes; the delta does it in 6 seconds.

For a 1 TB-class model in the Fireworks framing, their own measured numbers show 20.3 GiB deltas vs the 1024 GiB full snapshot, a ~50× reduction. PULSE's tighter, sparse encoding would push that further (extrapolating ~15 GB per delta, closer to ~65×). Either way, you are in a regime where shipping weights through commodity object storage stops being a hack and starts being the only sensible architecture.

We are not pretending this is finished. Here is the honest list.

#10184. Reachy Mini goes fully local

After building your Reachy Mini, you'll install the conversation app and start talking to it. Until now, you had to send your audio to a server. But not anymore. Today we'll walk you through running the whole stack locally.

This stack is powered by speech-to-speech, our cascaded VAD → STT → LLM → TTS pipeline that exposes a Realtime API-compatible /v1/realtime WebSocket. Once you launch the backend, point the robot at it from the UI.

Cascades are the most flexible option in the open-source landscape today, and with the right pieces they're also the fastest. We'll recommend the components we like best, but the whole point of a cascade is that you can swap them. New models drop every week.

This blog walks you through running conversations with Reachy Mini fully locally. No cloud, no API keys, no data leaving your machine. Here's a video showing this live:

To serve the LLM, we'll use Hugging Face's llama.cpp. If you need to install it, the simplest way is brew install llama.cpp or winget install llama.cpp, for more help, check the docs. First, we'll run:

And done! The first time it will download the model, subsequent launches are fast.

We'll begin by simply installing the library

Then, while we are serving the LLM in another terminal, we can simply run:

And you can start talking to the model through your terminal! The first time it will need to download Parakeet-TDT 0.6B v3 and Qwen3TTS, but subsequent launches are fast.

Here's a video showing the local conversation mode:

Now, after you've tried it in --mode local, you can run again the command without that option to serve speech-to-speech to the robot.

Once you have llama.cpp and speech-to-speech running, you can start the robot with the desktop app and launch the conversation app. In the UI from the conversation app, you need to choose the local mode by clicking on "edit connection" in the HF backend. Here's a video showing how to do it:

And you're done. You can start talking to your robot. Every stage of the pipeline is a trade-off: there are faster TTS models with lower quality, slower STT models with higher quality. We optimized for multilingual, you might want to optimize for a single language. The rest of the blog covers how to customize.

Hosted realtime backends are convenient, but running your own engine unlocks three things:

The speech-to-speech repo gives you all of that in a single CLI. It boots a WebSocket server at /v1/realtime that speaks the same protocol Reachy Mini already knows how to talk to.

A cascaded voice pipeline has four stages: VAD, STT, LLM, and TTS. For three of them, we pick solid defaults so you can focus on the LLM:

We are opinionated about these choices, feel free to swap them out for your own if you have a preference.

The LLM is the layer with the most impact on latency and overall performance of the system. We support two options: run a model locally (llama.cpp, MLX, Transformers, vLLM), or use a server with a Responses API (OpenAI, Gemini, HF Inference Endpoints, llama.cpp, vLLM, etc).

The main bottleneck in the system is LLM inference latency. To address that, we support external inference engines exposed through the Responses API protocol.

The speech-to-speech engine therefore supports a second mode where the LLM lives in a separate process as long as it speaks the Responses API protocol. You launch your model server in one terminal, you launch the voice loop in another terminal, and the two talk over HTTP.

Requires vLLM ≥ 0.21.0. Full support for the Responses API protocol, including tool-call streaming used by the speech-to-speech backend, landed in vLLM 0.21.0. Older versions will boot but trip up as soon as the assistant tries to call a tool.

When serving a model through vLLM for this pipeline, three flags are effectively required:

Terminal 1: vLLM inference server (Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507):

The --speculative-config line enables Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). It is optional, but it has a great impact on end-to-end latency. Leave it on whenever the model supports it.

Same protocol, but the model runs on a managed GPU on Hugging Face. Deploy any chat model as an Inference Endpoint, then point the voice loop at the endpoint URL:

If you don't want to manage your own endpoint, use an Inference Provider. Hugging Face routes your request to a third-party backend (e.g. Together, Fireworks, Replicate) with a single URL:

When you want to test against a frontier model with zero infra, point the same flag at OpenAI:

The --responses_api_* flags work the same for any provider that implements the protocol (OpenRouter, Together, Fireworks, …). Swap the base URL and the API key, keep the rest of the pipeline identical.

If you are on a Mac, MLX is the lowest-friction way to run a real model with sane latency. We recommend Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, which is small enough to feel instant on M-series chips and capable enough to hold a conversation.

The server listens on ws://127.0.0.1:8765/v1/realtime by default. Leave it running, connect the conversation app to the local backend, and you are talking to your robot.

Same idea, but using vanilla transformers. Use this if you are on a CUDA box, on Linux, or if you want to swap models freely without re-converting weights for MLX.

Tip. Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 is another good option for LLM because it gives a good speed/quality balance on a single consumer GPU. You can point --model_name at any HF model the backend supports — for example a larger Gemma, Qwen, or a Mistral.

If you are running the voice engine on your laptop and the conversation app on a Reachy Mini Wireless, the only thing that changes is the URL. Make sure the engine binds to a LAN address (not just 127.0.0.1) and use the laptop's IP from the robot when you select the IP in the UI.

If you don't know your IP, here's how to find it:

Look for "IPv4 Address" under your active adapter.

You want the 192.168.x.x or 10.x.x.x one. If you see 169.254.x.x, you're not actually on the network.

Star huggingface/speech-to-speech and pollen-robotics/reachy_mini_conversation_app, and come tell us in the discussions which open-source cascade you ended up running on your robot.

#10180. Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation

A live walkthrough of the Agents CLI eval loop, from a first run to regression tracking, model-backend experiments, and automated alerting

Building an agent that works on a demo is a different problem from building an agent that stays working across model upgrades, tool changes, and new conversation shapes. The first takes a weekend; the second takes a loop. A team writes test cases, runs them, grades them, reads what failed, changes the agent, and runs the cases again. If the score goes up, the change was good. If it goes down, revert. Over weeks of this, the agent inches toward the ceiling of what the model, tools, and prompt can do together. The quality-engineering name for this is hill-climbing.

The Agents CLI eval namespace was built around this loop. The commands are small and framework-agnostic: eval generate runs the agent against a dataset of cases, eval grade scores the generated traces, eval compare diffs two run results side by side, eval analyze clusters failures into themes, and eval optimize runs an automated hill-climbing pass on the agent's prompt.

Below: baseline → regression → model swap → scheduling and alerting.

The scaffold used throughout is the LangChain template that ships with Agents CLI v1.8.0. The setup is a single command:

The scaffold ships with an eval dataset at tests/eval/datasets/basic-dataset.json, a config at tests/eval/eval_config.yaml, and a custom LLM-as-judge metric at tests/eval/response_quality.py. The config declares the metric to run:

The metric grades each response on a 1-to-5 scale for accuracy, relevance, and clarity, using gemini-3.8-flash as the judge. The default dataset has a single trivial case, which is not enough for a hill-climb. The first thing we do is expand it to four cases that probe different behaviors:

Four cases: a greeting, a weather question the mock tool handles with the hardcoded foggy response, a weather question for a city the tool defaults on, and an off-topic question that the agent has to decide how to handle. This is a small dataset by design; the hill-climbing loop pays off when the dataset is small enough to run on every change.

With the dataset in place, we run eval generate to drive the agent against each case, then eval grade to score the resulting traces:

Mean 4.0 out of 5 across four cases, with a standard deviation of 1.41. That stdev tells us immediately that the cases are not scoring uniformly, which is a healthier starting point than a flat 5.0 across the board. A flat 5.0 either means the agent is perfect (unlikely) or the dataset is too easy to show variation. 4.0 with real spread is a hill to climb.

To demonstrate the loop, we introduce a realistic regression. A developer working across several agent projects accidentally pastes the wrong system prompt into our weather agent: a chef persona meant for a different codebase. In app/agent.py:

The change compiles, the agent still runs, and nothing in the pre-eval pipeline (lint, unit tests, type checks) catches it. Re-running the same eval generate plus eval grade sequence produces:

Mean 2.75, down from 4.0. The judge agrees with our intuition that a chef persona on a weather agent is a worse product than a general-purpose helpful assistant. The stdev also tightened from 1.41 to 0.96, consistent with the chef prompt pushing most cases toward the same mediocre range.

A 1.25-point drop on a 1-to-5 scale is substantial, and the kind of regression that can slip through code review when the diff looks small ("one string literal changed"). The loop surfaced the change at all, with a specific number attached to it, before the agent reached production.

Mean scores are a start; the per-case diff is where the hill-climb happens. eval compare reads two result files and produces a structured JSON diff:

The output lists which keys changed and which stayed the same:

The differences object has the full per-case breakdown with the baseline and candidate values side by side. For a hill-climbing workflow, we typically pipe the output through jq or a small Python script to extract the signal; the raw JSON is the complete evidence.

Walking the two result files and lining up the scores per case shows where the regression landed:

Three cases dropped, one held. The most important of the three is sf_weather: the chef persona pulled the model's attention away from the registered get_weather tool, so the agent stopped calling it and started making up weather values. Unit tests can't catch this: the code runs, the tool is still registered, but the model's behavior around it has shifted. Only an end-to-end eval that scores the response in context surfaces this.

The mean drop by itself (−1.25) is a clear signal, but the per-case breakdown is what tells the developer where to look. A one-line system-prompt change propagated through three different cases in three different ways: greeting lost a point on tone, sf_weather lost two on tool usage, off_topic lost two on scope creep.

A common hill-climbing question is whether a cheaper or faster model would do the job acceptably. For the LangChain template, the model is defined in app/agent.py:

We swap gemini-3.8-flash for gemini-2.5-flash (restoring the helpful system prompt first), re-run eval generate plus eval grade, and compare the two result files. The mean drops from 4.00 to 2.75, the same magnitude as the chef-prompt regression, but the per-case breakdown tells a completely different story:

The cheaper model matched 3.8-flash exactly on the greeting and rome_weather cases and lost a point on sf_weather (slightly less polished phrasing). The whole visible drop traces to off_topic, where the cheaper model refused with a hedge about the event "not having happened yet" (a training-cutoff artifact), and the judge marked it harshly.

The lesson is that the summary number is misleading. Look only at the mean and you'd call gemini-2.5-flash as bad as the chef prompt. Look at the per-case breakdown and you'd call it a reasonable swap for most of the agent's workload, with one case (handling out-of-scope questions about recent events) exposing a real limitation. If the production distribution of user questions matches the first three cases more than the fourth, the swap is worth considering. If off_topic-style questions are common, it is not.

Two caveats on this experiment. First, model swaps interact with the prompt: a prompt tuned for a stronger model often leaks capability when ported to a weaker one, so the right comparison is "weaker model with a prompt tuned for it" versus "stronger model with its own tuned prompt." Second, the Vertex AI Eval Service calls a judge model to grade the traces, and the judge is held constant across the comparison. Changing the judge is a different experiment and should be done separately.

Agents CLI does not ship a scheduler, but the eval commands are designed to drop into standard infrastructure. The pattern we can use here is a cron job or Cloud Scheduler trigger that runs eval generate plus eval grade on a cadence and writes the results to a persistent location:

A nightly run against a stable regression dataset catches drift from model updates, data changes in the agent's tools, and dependencies that shift under the agent's feet. For a production agent, the scheduled run also captures the model vendor's quiet upgrades, which can move the agent's behavior without any change on our side. The dataset for the scheduled run is typically larger than the one used in the inner loop (dozens to hundreds of cases rather than a few), since it only runs once a day.

The scheduled run produces a result file every day, but a file nobody looks at is not an alert. The pattern here can be a wrapper script that compares each new run's mean against a baseline (the previous run, or a committed known-good) and exits non-zero when the drop exceeds a threshold. The non-zero exit is what triggers the alert from the surrounding scheduler.

Running it against our regression demo (baseline 4.0, candidate 2.75 from the chef-prompt run):

And against an identical pair (self-compare):

The non-zero exit code is what a cron job, Cloud Scheduler, or GitHub Actions step picks up to send the alert.

For ADK projects, eval optimize runs an automated hill-climbing pass on the agent's prompt using the GEPA framework (not currently supported for the LangChain extension). The command takes a dataset and a target metric, proposes prompt variants, grades each one, keeps the variants that improve the metric, and iterates. The output is a set of candidate prompts ranked by their eval score, which a human then reviews and promotes to the agent definition.

Two things to understand about eval optimize. First, it is scoped to prompt optimization, not to arbitrary agent changes: the agent's tools, structure, and model stay fixed. Second, GEPA sometimes finds genuine improvements and sometimes finds prompt variants that score higher on the specific metric by overfitting to its wording. The reviewer is the control. For projects where the loop applies, the discipline is to run eval optimize on the regression dataset (where improvements are measurable) and to review the candidate prompts carefully before promotion.

A few patterns and anti-patterns from running this loop ourselves and watching teams do the same.

Lead with a small, representative dataset, not a comprehensive one. The temptation when starting an eval is to try to cover every edge case the agent will ever see. The result is a dataset that takes an hour to run and that nobody runs on a change. Four cases that run in under a minute, as above, exercise the main behaviors and get run on every change. A regression dataset of three hundred cases that runs for an hour becomes a release gate at best and shelfware at worst.

Snapshot result files, not scores. The score is a summary; the result file is the evidence. When a regression surfaces three weeks after a prompt change, having the full result JSON from before and after the change (not just the mean score) is what lets eval compare show the specific case that moved. The per-case breakdown in Step 4 above would not have been possible from scores alone.

Separate the dataset from its expectations. The dataset is the inputs. The eval config is the expectations. They evolve on different cadences: the dataset grows as new real-world cases surface in production, and the config evolves as the team's definition of "good" matures. Keeping them in separate files, both committed to version control, makes it clear which half changed when a score moves.

Treat summary metrics with suspicion. The model-swap experiment in Step 5 is the clearest example. The mean dropped by half a point, but the per-case breakdown showed the drop was concentrated in one case while the others held or improved. A team that only looked at the mean would have made the wrong call.

More evals do not automatically lead to more fixes. A recent controlled study we ran found that coding agents using agents-cli run four times as many evals as coding agents without it, but change the agent after an eval about as often as the baseline. The behavior gain comes from what the skills put into the build at the start, not from the inner iteration. Evals are necessary for quality, but the quality comes from acting on what the evals show.

Scaffold an Agents CLI project and run the first eval loop in a handful of commands:

The full eval namespace is documented at google.github.io/agents-cli/cli. The source code, including the first-party eval primitives, is at github.com/google/agents-cli.
